Breakfast is different around the world. In Brazil, people like coffee with milk, bread and butter, and fruit. In the US, many people like pancakes, eggs and bacon. In Japan, breakfast is rice, fish and miso soup. In England, people like tea and a "full English": eggs, beans, sausages and toast. What do you like?

Remote work is very common today. Many people work from home two or three days a week — this is called hybrid work. Why do people like it? Because they save time and money on their commute. But there are problems, too: some people feel lonely, and some people work too many hours. Where do remote workers work? At home, in coffee shops, in coworking spaces — and some travel the world as "digital nomads".

Brazil wastes a lot of food — millions of tons a year. Here are a few tips to waste less. First, make a grocery list and check what you already have. Don't buy too much bread: you can freeze some slices for later. Use old bananas in cakes or smoothies. Keep vegetables in the fridge, not in a bag. And don't throw away leftovers: a little rice and a few vegetables can become a delicious fried rice! Small changes save a lot of money, too.

A customer experience study found that most unhappy customers never complain — they just don't come back. That's bad for businesses, so many companies are happy when you complain politely! Be specific: "The coffee was cold" is better than "Everything was terrible." Say what you want: a new dish, a discount, a refund. And stay calm: people help nice customers more.

Many people hate small talk. "It's superficial," they say. But research in psychology suggests the opposite: short, friendly conversations with strangers — the barista, a neighbor, someone on the train — can make us happier and less lonely. In one study, commuters who talked to a stranger reported a more positive journey than those who sat in silence, even though most of them expected the opposite. Small talk is also the first step to deeper conversations: we rarely make friends or business contacts without it. The secret is curiosity. Ask open questions ("What brings you here?"), listen to the answer, and ask a follow-up. Safe topics include the weather, the place you're in, travel, food and work. Avoid politics, religion, money and personal appearance — at least until you know the person better.

Have you ever wondered why a trip makes you happier than a new phone? Psychologists who study happiness have found that spending money on experiences — travel, concerts, courses, dinners with friends — usually brings more lasting happiness than spending on things. One reason is adaptation: we get used to new objects quickly, but memories of experiences often get better with time. Another reason is connection: experiences are usually shared with other people and become part of our identity and our stories. "I've climbed a volcano" says more about who you are than "I've bought a new TV." Of course, things matter too — but next time you have some extra money, consider buying a memory instead of an object.

Tipping is one of the most confusing parts of traveling. In the United States, servers depend on tips because their salaries are low, so you're supposed to leave 15 to 20 percent in restaurants. Not tipping is seen as very rude. In Japan, it's the opposite: tipping can be considered strange or even insulting, because good service is simply expected. In most of Europe, a service charge is often included in the bill, and leaving a few extra coins is a nice gesture but not required. In Brazil, restaurants usually add 10% to the bill, and you can choose not to pay it — although most people do. The golden rule? Check the local custom before you travel, and when you're not sure, ask: "Is service included?"

The way you open and close an email shows your tone. For a formal email to someone you don't know, start with "Dear Mr. Lee" or "Dear Ms. Santos". If you don't know the name, "Dear Hiring Manager" is better than "To whom it may concern", which sounds old-fashioned. For colleagues, "Hi Ana" is perfect. Close formal emails with "Kind regards" or "Best regards". "Cheers" is friendly, especially in the UK and Australia, but don't use it with a new client. And please — never write "Kisses" or "Hugs" in a business email, even if Brazilians do it with friends!

In many English-speaking workplaces, titles are becoming less common. Tech companies in Silicon Valley are famous for their informal culture: the CEO is "Mark" or "Sundar", and nobody wears a tie. Many universities and hospitals, however, still prefer titles like "Professor" and "Dr.", especially with students and patients. In the UK, older generations often expect "Mr." or "Mrs." until they say otherwise. Another change is the use of "Ms." instead of "Mrs." or "Miss": it doesn't reveal whether a woman is married, and it's now the standard in professional situations. Some people prefer gender-neutral titles like "Mx." The safest strategy? Follow the other person's lead. If someone signs an email "Jennifer", you can reply "Hi Jennifer". If they sign "Dr. Jennifer Adams", start with "Dear Dr. Adams".

Some people stay in the same place for an incredibly long time. In Japan, a hotel called Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan has welcomed guests since the year 705 — it's been run by the same family for more than fifty generations. In the UK, a man named Bob Tanner delivered newspapers for 70 years in the same town. And in Brazil, many small businesses have passed from parents to children for decades. Why do people stay? Researchers say a sense of belonging is one of the main reasons: when you've known your neighbors for years and your customers since they were children, leaving feels like losing part of your identity. In a world where people change jobs every few years, these stories feel almost magical.

Have you ever noticed that unfinished tasks stay in your head, while finished ones disappear? This is called the Zeigarnik effect, after a psychologist who observed that waiters remembered unpaid orders perfectly — but forgot them as soon as the customers had paid. Our brains keep "open" tasks active, which can cause stress. Productivity experts suggest a simple solution: write everything down. Once a task is on a list, your brain can relax a little. At the end of the day, look at what you've already done, not only at what you haven't done yet. Celebrating small wins — "I've just answered all my emails!" — keeps you motivated.

Many adults believe that they can't learn new skills after a certain age. "I couldn't learn a language now — my brain is too old," they say. Neuroscience says otherwise. Thanks to neuroplasticity, our brains can create new connections throughout our lives. Children may learn some things faster, but adults have advantages too: they can organize their study, understand grammar rules and connect new information to what they already know. Consider Dona Neusa from Minas Gerais: she couldn't read until she was 70. She went back to school, and two years later she was able to read her first novel. "I've been able to do things I never imagined," she says. Her secret? "I never gave up."

Do you want someone to like you more? Ask them for a favor. It sounds strange, but it's a well-known psychological phenomenon called the Ben Franklin effect. In the 18th century, Benjamin Franklin had a political rival who didn't like him. Instead of being extra nice to him, Franklin wrote a polite letter asking if he could borrow a rare book from the man's library. The rival lent it, Franklin returned it with a warm thank-you note, and the two became friends. Psychologists explain that when we do someone a favor, our brain looks for a reason: "I helped this person, so I must like them." The lesson? Small favors — "Could you recommend a good restaurant?" — can build relationships. Just don't ask for too many!

What can we learn from people who have lived for a century? Journalists and researchers who have interviewed centenarians around the world have noticed some common advice. And almost all of them mentioned relationships: "If I were you, I'd call my friends more often. In the end, people are what matter." Interestingly, very few of them talked about work or success. Have you ever had a phone repaired, only to be told that it's cheaper to buy a new one? You're not alone. For years, many manufacturers have made it difficult for customers to get their devices fixed: special screws, glued batteries, and parts that only official stores can buy. Now, a global movement called "Right to Repair" is fighting back. The European Union and several US states have passed laws requiring companies to sell spare parts and repair manuals for many products. Supporters say this will reduce electronic waste — one of the fastest-growing types of waste in the world — and save consumers money. In Brazil, small repair shops have always been part of the culture: we get our shoes resoled, our clothes altered and our appliances fixed. Maybe the rest of the world is finally catching up.

Some people would rather work in a quiet room alone; others prefer a busy open office full of conversation. Psychologists often describe this difference using the terms introvert and extrovert. Introverts usually prefer deep one-on-one conversations to big group meetings, and many would rather write an email than make a phone call. Extroverts, on the other hand, often get energy from people and prefer brainstorming out loud. Most people, however, are somewhere in the middle — sometimes called ambiverts. The problem is that many workplaces are designed for extroverts: open-plan offices, constant meetings and team-building events. Smart companies now offer options: quiet zones, "no-meeting" days and flexible work. After all, people do their best work when they can choose how they work.

We all know the feeling: you need to finish a report, but you keep checking your phone, cleaning your desk, or watching "just one more" video. Most people think procrastination is about being lazy, but psychologists disagree. Research suggests that procrastination is mainly about avoiding negative emotions — boredom, anxiety, fear of failure. When a task makes us feel bad, our brain decides to look for something more pleasant. So how can we stop procrastinating? Who do you trust more: an advertisement or a friend? For most people, the answer is obvious. Marketing studies have repeatedly shown that personal recommendations are among the most trusted forms of advertising. That's why so many businesses invest in referral programs: "Recommend a friend and you both get 20% off." Online reviews have become a digital version of word of mouth — but they have a problem. Experts suggest reading the three-star reviews, which are often the most honest, looking for specific details, and checking whether the same reviewer has written many similar reviews. Coffee is drunk by billions of people every day, but where did it come from? According to legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia, when a goat herder noticed that his goats became very energetic after eating some red berries. The plant was later taken to Yemen, where coffee was first prepared as a drink. In the 18th century, coffee seeds were brought to Brazil — legend says they were secretly given to a Portuguese officer in French Guiana. Today, Brazil is the world's largest coffee producer: around a third of the world's coffee is grown here, mainly in Minas Gerais, São Paulo and Espírito Santo. The beans are harvested between May and September and are exported to more than 100 countries.

Here are five quick ways to spot fake news. One: check the source. Is it a website you know? Two: read beyond the headline — clickbait headlines are designed to make you angry or scared. Three: check the date — old stories are often shared as if they were new. Four: look for evidence. Are there names, data, links to studies? Five: if it seems too good, or too terrible, to be true, it probably is. And remember: it's believed that people are more likely to share news that confirms what they already think. So be extra careful with stories you love!

"A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes." This famous quote — which, ironically, is often wrongly attributed to Mark Twain — describes a real phenomenon. A well-known study by researchers at MIT analyzed more than 100,000 stories shared on Twitter between 2006 and 2017. It was found that false stories were much more likely to be retweeted than true ones and reached people significantly faster. Why? The researchers believe that fake news is usually more surprising and emotional, and people love sharing things that are new and shocking. Interestingly, the study suggested that humans, not bots, were mainly responsible for the spread. With AI tools now able to create realistic fake images and videos, experts say media literacy — the ability to evaluate information critically — is one of the most important skills of the 21st century.

If you read ten pages a day, you'll read about a dozen books a year. If you save ten reais a day, you'll have more than 3,600 reais in twelve months. This is the logic behind "small habits", an idea popularized by writers like James Clear. The concept is simple: small actions, repeated consistently, produce big results over time. It works the other way too: if you sleep one hour less every night, you'll lose more than 300 hours of sleep in a year — and your health will suffer. Experts suggest using "if-then" plans to build new habits: "If it's 7 a.m., I'll drink a glass of water." "If I feel like checking social media, I'll do five push-ups first." Studies show that people who make if-then plans are much more likely to achieve their goals.

If you suddenly became a millionaire, would you be happier? Most people say yes immediately. But research on lottery winners shows a more complicated picture. In a famous study from the 1970s, psychologists compared lottery winners with ordinary people and found that, after some time, the winners weren't much happier — they had adapted to their new lives. More recent research suggests that money does increase happiness, especially when it removes financial stress. But how you use it matters. People who spend money on experiences, on other people, or on buying time — like paying someone to do the chores they hate — tend to report more satisfaction than those who buy expensive things. So, if you won the lottery tomorrow, what would make you happier: a sports car, or more time with the people you love?

"I want to improve my English" is a wish, not a goal. Unless a goal is specific, it's very hard to achieve. That's why many coaches recommend SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Compare "I'll study more" with "I'll study English for 30 minutes a day, five days a week, until I reach B2 by December." The second one tells you exactly what to do, how to measure it and when the deadline is. Experts also suggest breaking big goals into milestones. As soon as you reach one, celebrate — and then move to the next. Keep track of your progress in a notebook or app, in case you lose motivation on difficult days: looking back at how far you've come is one of the best ways to keep going.

Many English learners feel fast progress at the beginning: every week, they can say new things. Then, around B1, something strange happens: progress seems to stop. This is known as the intermediate plateau. It happens because you can already communicate in most everyday situations, so you're no longer forced to learn new language. You keep using the same words and structures that "work". How can you break the plateau? Teachers suggest three things. First, consume more authentic content — podcasts, series, YouTube channels and articles about topics you love. Second, push yourself to use new vocabulary on purpose, even if you make mistakes. Third, get feedback: record yourself, write texts and ask someone to correct them. The plateau isn't a sign that you've stopped learning. It's a sign that you're ready for the next level.

For decades, the typical career path was simple: study, get a stable job, climb the career ladder and retire. Today, many workers are questioning that model. Interestingly, purpose doesn't require a "heroic" job. Hospital cleaners who see their role as helping patients recover often report high satisfaction. In other words, meaning doesn't only come from what we do, but from how we think about what we do.

Why do some people succeed while others with the same talent give up? Psychologist Angela Duckworth spent years studying this question with groups as different as military cadets, salespeople and children in spelling competitions. Her answer was a quality she called "grit": a combination of passion and perseverance for long-term goals. According to her research, grit was often a better predictor of success than talent or IQ. Gritty people aren't necessarily the most intelligent; they're the ones who keep going after failure. The good news is that grit can be developed. Parents and teachers can encourage children to finish what they start, let them experience small failures, and teach them to see mistakes as part of learning. Some critics argue that the concept is too similar to older ideas like conscientiousness, but the message remains popular: talent is important, but effort counts twice.

Why do some ideas disappear after a few months while others change the world? Sociologist Everett Rogers studied this question in the 1960s and developed a theory called the "diffusion of innovations". According to Rogers, new ideas spread through a population in stages. First come the innovators, a tiny group who love taking risks. Next, the early adopters try the idea and, crucially, tell others about it. Only after that does the majority follow — first the "early majority", then the more skeptical "late majority". Finally, the "laggards" accept the change, often reluctantly. Smartphones followed this pattern: in 2007 they were expensive gadgets for tech fans; a decade later, even grandparents were sending voice messages. Fads, on the other hand, usually never get past the early adopters. The difference? Real innovations solve a problem people actually have.

Most interview questions aren't really about what they seem to ask. "Tell me about yourself" isn't an invitation to share your life story; the interviewer wants a short, relevant summary that explains why you're right for the job. "Why do you want to leave your current job?" is testing your professionalism: criticizing your current boss is a red flag, even if your boss is terrible. "Where do you see yourself in five years?" checks whether your goals match what the company can offer — and whether you're likely to stay. And the famous "What's your biggest weakness?" is about self-awareness: the worst answers are "I don't have any" or the cliché "I'm a perfectionist" without any example. Experts suggest preparing three or four short stories about your experience that you can adapt to different questions. When you understand the question behind the question, you can answer what the interviewer really wants to know.

Here are a few rules I teach everyone. One: before you buy something that isn't essential, wait 48 hours. Most impulse purchases don't survive the wait. In Brazil, Pix — the instant payment system launched by the Central Bank in 2020 — became one of the most widely used payment methods in the country in a remarkably short time. The question is not whether cash will disappear, but how quickly — and who will pay the price.

The marshmallow test is one of the most famous experiments in psychology. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, researchers at Stanford University offered preschool children a choice: eat one treat now, or wait alone for about fifteen minutes and get two. Years later, follow-up studies suggested that the children who had waited tended to have better school results and other positive outcomes. The idea spread quickly: self-control, it seemed, was a key to success. Since then, however, the story has become more complicated. The original groups were small and mostly came from families connected to the university. In 2018, a larger study with a more diverse group of children found a much weaker connection, and much of it seemed to be explained by factors like family income and education. Other researchers have shown that children wait longer when they trust the adult who made the promise. So the test may measure not only willpower, but also experience: if promises in your life have often been broken, eating the marshmallow now is a rational choice.

When we see a brilliant musician, athlete or entrepreneur, we often assume they were simply born with a special talent. But researchers who study expertise tell a different story. In a famous study in the 1990s, psychologist Anders Ericsson looked at violin students at a music academy in Berlin. He found that the best students had practiced significantly more hours than the others — and, crucially, that they had practiced in a specific way. Ericsson called it "deliberate practice": working on your weaknesses, getting regular feedback and constantly pushing beyond your comfort zone. Writer Malcolm Gladwell later popularized the idea as the "10,000-hour rule", although Ericsson himself said that the number was not a magic rule. Since then, other scientists have argued that factors like genes, starting age and opportunity also matter. Still, the main lesson remains: behind most "overnight successes" there are years of invisible, focused work.

Why do some apologies make things better while others make them worse? Researchers who study communication have identified several elements that make an apology effective. The most important one, according to some studies, is acknowledging responsibility: saying clearly "It was my fault" or "I made a mistake". The second is offering to repair the damage. Expressing regret ("I'm sorry") matters too, but on its own it often isn't enough. Interestingly, long explanations can backfire: if you spend too much time explaining why something happened, people may hear it as an excuse. The worst apologies are "non-apologies" — phrases like "I'm sorry if you were offended" or "Mistakes were made", which avoid taking real responsibility. Public figures and companies use them all the time, and audiences usually notice. The lesson? A good apology is short, specific and focused on the other person, not on yourself.

For more than a decade, influencer marketing has been one of the fastest-growing areas of advertising. Brands pay creators — from celebrities with millions of followers to "micro-influencers" with just a few thousand — to recommend their products. The logic is simple: people trust people more than they trust ads. But audiences have become more skeptical. Many followers now know that a glowing review may be a paid partnership, and regulators in several countries require influencers to label sponsored posts clearly. In this context, a new trend has appeared: "de-influencing". Creators post videos explaining which popular products are not worth the money and suggesting cheaper alternatives. Ironically, de-influencing has itself become a marketing strategy, as some brands now position themselves as the honest alternative. The lesson for marketers is clear: in a world full of advertising, authenticity is the most valuable — and the most difficult — thing to sell.

Some products are so ordinary that we forget they were once revolutionary. Take the ballpoint pen, which was patented in 1938 by László Bíró, a Hungarian journalist who was tired of smudged ink. Or the shopping cart, which was invented in the 1930s by a supermarket owner in Oklahoma whose customers stopped shopping when their baskets got too heavy. At first, shoppers refused to use carts — men thought they looked weak and women thought they looked like baby strollers — so the owner hired actors to push them around the store. In Brazil, an example of a product that changed daily life is the flip-flop. Havaianas, which were created in 1962, were inspired by Japanese zori sandals, and for decades they were seen as cheap shoes for poor people. A clever marketing strategy in the 1990s transformed them into a fashion item that celebrities wear all over the world. The lesson? A good product is important, but the story that people tell about it can matter just as much.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, millions of people suddenly needed to understand complex scientific ideas: how viruses spread, how vaccines work, what an "R number" is. Scientists who could explain these ideas clearly became incredibly influential, while those who used technical language often failed to reach the public — and misinformation filled the gap. Experts in science communication say there are a few simple rules. First, start with why it matters to the audience, not with the method. Second, use analogies: comparing the immune system to a security team or DNA to a recipe book helps people make sense of abstract ideas. Third, avoid jargon, or explain it the first time you use it. Fourth, tell stories: people remember narratives far better than statistics. Finally, be honest about uncertainty. Saying "we don't know yet, but we're going to find out" builds more trust than pretending to have all the answers. In the future, many experts believe these communication skills will be as important for scientists as research itself.

Many people hate networking because they think it's about selling themselves. It isn't. Good networking is about being curious. Here are my top tips. First, arrive early — it's much easier to start conversations when the room is half empty. Second, prepare three open questions, like "What are you working on at the moment?" Third, listen more than you talk; people remember how you made them feel, not your job title. Fourth, don't stay with the same person all night — after ten minutes, politely move on. And finally, follow up within 48 hours. Send a short message mentioning something specific you talked about. That's how a five-minute conversation becomes a long-term relationship.

Who is most likely to help you find your next job: your best friend, or someone you met once at a conference? Surprisingly, research suggests it's often the second. In a classic 1973 study, sociologist Mark Granovetter interviewed people who had recently changed jobs and found that many of them had heard about the opportunity through acquaintances — people they saw only occasionally — rather than close friends. He called this "the strength of weak ties". The explanation is simple: your close friends usually know the same people and hear about the same opportunities as you. Acquaintances, on the other hand, move in different circles, so they bring new information. A large study published in 2022, which analyzed data from millions of LinkedIn users, found further support for the idea, showing that moderately weak connections were the most useful for job mobility. So the next time you're at an event and feel tempted to talk only to your colleagues, remember: the stranger by the coffee machine might be the key to your next opportunity.

For a long time, many workplaces were designed for one type of brain. Job interviews rewarded people who were good at small talk and eye contact, open-plan offices were full of noise, and instructions were often vague. As a result, many talented neurodivergent people — including autistic people and people with ADHD or dyslexia — struggled to find or keep jobs. In recent years, some large companies have started neurodiversity hiring programs. Instead of traditional interviews, candidates might spend a few days solving real problems, and managers receive training on how to give clear, direct feedback. Several of these companies report that neurodivergent employees bring valuable strengths, such as pattern recognition, attention to detail, creative problem-solving and deep focus. Advocates point out, however, that the goal shouldn't only be productivity. "Inclusion isn't about finding hidden superpowers," one autistic activist explains. "It's about accepting that people think differently — and that's normal."

What if everything you needed — work, school, shops, a doctor, a park — was within a 15-minute walk or bike ride from your home? That's the idea behind the "15-minute city", a concept developed by the urbanist Carlos Moreno and adopted by Paris and other cities around the world. Supporters argue that it's likely to reduce traffic, pollution and stress, while making neighborhoods more lively and social. In Paris, the city has created hundreds of kilometers of new bike lanes and turned some streets around schools into car-free zones. Critics, however, say the idea may not work in places with low population density, where shops and jobs are far apart. Others worry that it could increase housing prices in well-designed neighborhoods, pushing poorer residents out. Some online conspiracy theories have even claimed, without evidence, that 15-minute cities are a plan to restrict people's freedom of movement. The debate is bound to continue — but as cities grow and the climate crisis worsens, many planners believe that shorter, greener journeys are the future.

Today, let's talk about simple inventions that might change millions of lives. Take the solar-powered lamp, for example. In places without electricity, families often use kerosene lamps, which are expensive and dangerous. A cheap solar lamp could save money and prevent fires. Or consider low-cost water filters made from clay and sawdust. The inventors must have asked themselves: what materials do local people already have? That's the secret. The best solutions often aren't the most high-tech ones. They're the ones that people can afford, repair and actually use. So the next time you face a problem, ask yourself: could the answer be simpler than I think?

In 1912, a book dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought a strange manuscript from a collection in Italy. The book, which is now kept at Yale University, has about 240 pages full of drawings of unknown plants, astronomical diagrams and women bathing in green pools. But the strangest thing is the text: it's written in an alphabet that nobody has ever been able to read. Carbon dating has shown that the parchment must have been made in the early 15th century. So who wrote it, and why? Some researchers believe it might be written in a lost natural language. Others think it could be a code designed to hide secret medical or alchemical knowledge. Some skeptics argue that it can't contain real meaning at all: it might have been a clever hoax, created to sell to a rich collector. Over the years, linguists, cryptographers and even AI programs have tried to decode it, and several people have claimed to have solved the mystery — but none of their solutions has been widely accepted. For now, the Voynich manuscript remains one of the most famous unsolved puzzles in the world.

For many young professionals, an unexpected phone call feels almost like an emergency. Surveys in the UK and the US have found that a large number of people under 35 avoid answering calls from unknown numbers, and many feel anxious when they have to make a call. Some even rehearse what they're going to say before dialing. Why? Researchers point to several reasons. Text messages and emails give us time to think and edit; phone calls happen in real time, with no chance to delete a mistake. Calls can also feel intrusive: they interrupt whatever you're doing. And for people speaking a second language, the lack of facial expressions and gestures makes understanding much harder. However, many managers say that phone calls are still the fastest way to solve complex problems and build relationships. A five-minute call can save twenty emails. The solution? Practice. Experts suggest preparing a few key phrases, keeping a notepad ready and remembering that it's completely normal to say: "Sorry, could you repeat that?"

Most of us want to be more productive, but we often look for big solutions: a new job, a new app, a complete change of routine. Productivity experts suggest the opposite. If you make small, specific changes, they'll add up over time. Here are some research-backed ideas. If you check your email first thing in the morning, you'll spend the day reacting to other people's priorities — so start with your most important task instead. When you work on a difficult task, turn off notifications: some studies suggest that it can take a long time to fully refocus after an interruption. Use the "two-minute rule": if something takes less than two minutes, do it immediately. And unless you have a very good reason, don't multitask. Our brains don't really do two things at once; they switch quickly between them, and every switch costs energy. As the saying goes, "If you chase two rabbits, you'll catch neither."

In 1935, a new American bomber plane crashed during a test flight, killing two of its crew. The investigation found that the pilots hadn't made a mechanical error — they had simply forgotten one step: they hadn't released a lock on the controls. The plane was considered "too complex for one person to fly". Instead of giving up, test pilots created a simple solution: a checklist. With it, the plane went on to fly safely for millions of miles. Decades later, surgeon and writer Atul Gawande argued in his book The Checklist Manifesto that the same idea could save lives in hospitals. A study coordinated by the World Health Organization in eight hospitals around the world found that a simple surgical safety checklist was associated with a significant reduction in complications and deaths. The checklist didn't teach surgeons anything new; it made sure that the basic steps — confirming the patient's identity, checking allergies, counting instruments — weren't overlooked. The lesson goes beyond medicine: experts don't fail because they lack knowledge, but because even the best people sometimes forget the obvious.

In Brazil, a large part of the waste that gets recycled is collected not by machines or big companies, but by people: the catadores, or waste pickers. Estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of Brazilians work in this activity, many of them in cooperatives. For decades, their work was largely invisible and badly paid. In recent years, however, their role has been increasingly recognized. A national policy on solid waste, approved in 2010, encouraged cities to include waste picker cooperatives in their recycling systems, and in many places their work is now being formally contracted by local governments. Aluminum cans are a famous success story: Brazil has recycled a very high proportion of its aluminum cans for many years, largely thanks to the work of catadores. Challenges remain — many waste pickers still work in difficult and unsafe conditions — but their story shows that environmental solutions can't be separated from social justice.

Misunderstandings between cultures are rarely about grammar. More often, they come from different expectations about how directly people should speak. Researchers on intercultural communication describe some cultures — like the Netherlands, Germany or Israel — as "low-context": people tend to say exactly what they mean, and the words carry most of the message. Other cultures — like Japan, China or much of Latin America, including Brazil — are often described as "high-context": a lot of the meaning comes from tone, relationships and what is not said. This can cause confusion. When a British colleague says "That's an interesting idea", they may actually mean "I don't agree". When a Brazilian says "Let's meet up sometime!", it may be a friendly expression rather than a real plan. Experts suggest a simple strategy for international teams: when in doubt, check. Paraphrase what you understood ("So you'd like me to...?"), ask for concrete details (dates, numbers, next steps) and never assume that silence means agreement.

"Be the change you wish to see in the world," said Gandhi. Or did he? This famous quote appears on posters, mugs and social media posts, but researchers who have studied Gandhi's writings say he never wrote or said those exact words. He did write something with a similar idea, but in a much longer and more complex sentence. The same thing has happened to many other famous people. Einstein is often quoted as saying that doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results is "the definition of insanity" — but there's no evidence he ever said it. And Marie Antoinette almost certainly never told hungry French peasants to "eat cake". Why do fake quotes spread so easily? Psychologists suggest that a sentence seems more true and more wise when it's attached to a famous name. So the next time someone tells you that a celebrity said something brilliant, you might want to ask a simple question: "Where exactly did they say it?"

She had grown up on a small farm in Paraná, and she had watched her parents struggle to sell their vegetables at fair prices. She had been thinking about the problem for years. When she finally quit her job, she had saved enough money for only six months. By the time she found her first investor, she had been rejected more than thirty times. Today, the app connects more than 40,000 farmers.

We often celebrate young geniuses: the teenage tech founder, the 20-year-old Olympic champion. But many remarkable people achieved success much later. Before she published the first Harry Potter book at 32, J.K. Rowling had been rejected by numerous publishers and had been living as a single mother on very little money. The fashion designer Vera Wang had worked as a journalist and figure skater before she designed her first dress at 40. Colonel Sanders had tried many careers — and failed at several — before he started franchising his fried chicken in his sixties. In Brazil, the writer Cora Coralina had been writing poetry for most of her life, but her first book wasn't published until she was 75. Researchers who study creativity suggest that there are different types of creators: some make their breakthroughs early through bold experiments, while others need decades of accumulated experience. The lesson? If you haven't found your path by 30 — or 50 — you're in very good company.

My patients often ask me: "If you could recommend just one change, what would it be?" My answer is almost always the same: sleep. If most adults slept seven to nine hours a night, we would see fewer cases of heart disease, depression and obesity. The second change would be movement. You don't need to run marathons. If you walked thirty minutes a day, you would reduce your risk of many diseases. And if people spent less time looking at screens before bed, they might fall asleep faster. Many patients tell me they wish they had more time to take care of themselves. But often, it isn't time they need — it's a few small, consistent decisions.

Why do people in some parts of the world live much longer than others? Journalist Dan Buettner, working with researchers and demographers, identified five regions with unusually high numbers of centenarians and called them the "Blue Zones": Okinawa (Japan), Sardinia (Italy), Nicoya (Costa Rica), Ikaria (Greece) and Loma Linda (California, USA). In these places, people don't go to the gym or follow strict diets. Instead, they share some simple habits. They move naturally throughout the day — walking, gardening, doing housework. They eat mostly plants, especially beans, and they stop eating before they feel completely full. They have a strong sense of purpose and close family and community ties. If we all lived like this, would we live to 100? Not necessarily — genes and healthcare also matter, and some researchers have questioned parts of the data. But the main message is hard to argue with: if our daily lives included more movement, better food and stronger relationships, most of us would probably be healthier and happier.

In a supermarket in California, researchers once set up a table with samples of jam. On some days, the table offered 24 flavors; on other days, only 6. The large display attracted more visitors, but when only 6 flavors were offered, a much higher percentage of people actually bought a jar. This famous experiment, published in 2000, helped popularize an idea that psychologist Barry Schwartz called "the paradox of choice": having too many options can make it harder to decide and less satisfying once we have decided. When we have many alternatives, we worry that we might have chosen badly, and we imagine how much better the other options might have been. Later studies have shown that the effect doesn't always appear — it depends on how complex the options are and how much we know about them. Still, many experts suggest a practical strategy for everyday decisions: reduce your options to two or three, decide what really matters to you, and remember that "good enough" is often better than "perfect". As Schwartz has argued, people who look for the absolute best option are often less happy with their choices than people who are satisfied with a good one.

Research suggests that we form an impression of someone's face in a fraction of a second — some studies say about a tenth of a second. We tend to judge whether someone is trustworthy, competent or friendly almost instantly. The problem is that these snap judgements are heavily influenced by bias. For example, we tend to see people who look like us as more trustworthy, and we'll often assume that attractive people are also smarter — something psychologists call the halo effect. The good news is that first impressions aren't fixed. If we keep meeting someone and they keep behaving in a way that contradicts our first judgement, we'll eventually update our opinion. The key is to stay curious and to be aware of our own biases.

Imagine meeting two job candidates. One walks in confidently, makes eye contact and tells a funny story. The other speaks quietly and looks down. Most of us would instinctively prefer the first — even though nothing we've seen tells us who would actually do the job better. Psychologists have identified several reasons why our judgements of other people tend to be unreliable. One is the halo effect: when someone has one attractive quality, we'll tend to assume they have others too. Another is the fundamental attribution error: when other people behave badly, we tend to blame their personality ("He's rude"), but when we behave badly, we blame the situation ("I was tired"). Culture also plays a role. In some cultures, direct eye contact signals honesty; in others, it can come across as disrespectful. What seems confident in one country may seem arrogant in another. None of this means we should ignore our instincts completely. But it does suggest that we should hold our first impressions lightly, look for evidence, and give people the same benefit of the doubt that we would want them to give us.

One of the most common things people tell us is that they've drifted apart from friends without any real conflict. Life just gets in the way: people move, have children, change jobs. Research suggests that adult friendships need regular contact to survive — not necessarily long conversations, but small gestures, like sending a message or catching up over coffee. Another key factor is how people deal with conflict. Friends who fall out but then talk openly and make up often end up closer than before. On the other hand, friendships where people keep putting up with things they don't like, without saying anything, tend to fade. So my advice is simple: reach out, and if something bothers you, bring it up — kindly.

In recent years, several surveys in the United States and other countries have suggested that adults have fewer close friends than they used to. Some commentators have even started talking about a "friendship recession". The reasons are complex. People work longer hours, move more often for jobs and spend more time online. Many say they simply don't have time to catch up with friends, and that friendships slowly fade without anyone falling out. Researchers also point out that making new friends as an adult is harder than at school or university, where we meet the same people every day without trying. One frequently quoted study by Jeffrey Hall estimated that it takes around 50 hours of time together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, and more than 200 hours to become close friends. That's a lot of coffees. However, there are reasons for optimism. Many people are deliberately making time for friendship: joining running clubs, book clubs and volunteer groups, where repeated contact happens naturally. As one participant put it, "I used to wait for friendships to happen. Now I put the effort in — and I've never felt less lonely."

Today, many workplaces have four or even five generations working side by side. Managers often ask me whether younger employees are really that different. My answer: slightly, but nowhere near as much as the headlines suggest. Surveys show that, on average, younger workers tend to value flexibility and feedback a bit more, while older workers tend to value stability. But when you look at what people want most — fair pay, respect and meaningful work — the generations are remarkably similar. The bigger problem is stereotypes. The more we assume that a 60-year-old can't learn new technology, or that a 25-year-old won't stay in a job, the worse our teams work. The best approach is mentoring in both directions: older employees share experience, younger ones share new tools. The more they learn from each other, the better.

Every generation seems to believe that the next one is lazier, more selfish and more addicted to whatever technology is new. Similar complaints about young people can be found in texts from centuries ago. Today, the target is often Generation Z, described in headlines as anxious, glued to their phones and unwilling to work hard. But how much of this is true? The data paint a more complex picture. On the one hand, young people today do spend considerably more time online than previous generations did at the same age, and surveys in several countries suggest that reported levels of anxiety among teenagers have risen. On the other hand, many members of Gen Z drink far less alcohol and smoke much less than their parents did as teenagers, and they're often just as interested in meaningful work. Economic conditions matter too. In many countries, housing has become far more expensive relative to income, making it nowhere near as easy for young people to reach traditional milestones like buying a home. Researchers increasingly argue that differences between generations are often less about character and more about circumstances. Put simply: the more you change the world young people grow up in, the more their choices will change too.

Students often ask me why academic writing is so full of words like "may", "suggest" and "appear". Isn't it better to be confident? The answer is that good researchers try not to claim more than their evidence shows. If one study finds that coffee drinkers live longer, a careful scientist won't write "Coffee makes you live longer." They'll write something like "The results suggest that moderate coffee consumption may be associated with a lower risk of mortality." It's less exciting, but it's more honest. The study can't prove that coffee is the cause — perhaps coffee drinkers also tend to have other healthy habits. Hedging isn't weakness. It's precision. And in a world full of exaggerated headlines, I'd argue we need much more of it.

In 2008, computer scientist and essayist Paul Graham proposed a "hierarchy of disagreement" — a pyramid showing different ways people argue, from the least to the most useful. At the bottom is name-calling: attacking the person rather than the idea ("You're an idiot"). Slightly higher is responding to tone ("Why are you being so aggressive?"), which avoids the actual argument. In the middle is contradiction: simply stating the opposite view without evidence. Near the top is counterargument — giving reasons and evidence for a different position — and at the very top is refutation: identifying exactly where the other person's argument goes wrong and explaining why. Graham's model has been widely shared online, perhaps because many public debates seem to be stuck at the bottom of the pyramid. Social media, which rewards quick and emotional reactions, arguably makes things worse. Psychologists who study conflict suggest a few habits that may help: listen to understand rather than to reply, summarize the other person's view before responding ("So you're saying..."), and look for common ground. Disagreeing well doesn't mean avoiding conflict. It means making conflict productive.

Let me paint a picture of 2035. By then, many of the jobs we know today will have changed dramatically — and some will have disappeared altogether. Millions of people will be working in roles that don't exist yet. Most of us won't be doing the same job for forty years; instead, we'll be retraining several times throughout our careers. In their book The 100-Year Life, Lynda Gratton and Andrew Scott argue that as life expectancy increases, the traditional three-stage life — education, work, retirement — will no longer make sense for many people. If you're likely to live to 90 or 100, you probably won't be able to stop working at 60 and live on your savings for forty years. Instead, the authors predict a multi-stage life. People will be studying, working, taking breaks and retraining in different combinations throughout their lives. Someone might work in finance until 40, take a year off to travel, retrain as a teacher and then set up a small business at 60. By the time they finally retire, they will have had several careers, not one. This has big implications. Governments will need to rethink pensions and education. Companies will have to stop seeing older workers as a cost and start seeing them as an asset. And individuals will need to invest in what the authors call "intangible assets": skills, health, relationships and the ability to adapt. The good news? A longer life means more time to try new things. The challenge is that most of our institutions were designed for a much shorter one.

Many famous success stories begin with a plan that went wrong. In the early 2000s, a small company called Odeo was going to become a major podcasting platform. Then Apple added podcasts to iTunes, and the founders realized their product would never compete. Instead of giving up, they held a brainstorming session, and one employee suggested a simple service for sharing short status updates. That idea became Twitter. Similarly, the founders of Slack were originally building an online game called Glitch. The game failed, but the internal chat tool the team had built to communicate turned out to be far more valuable than the game itself. Nobody at the time thought it would become one of the most widely used workplace tools in the world. Psychologists say that people who handle these moments well tend to share two qualities: they're flexible enough to change direction, and they see failure as information rather than as a final verdict. In other words, the plan you were going to follow might not be the plan you were supposed to follow. Sometimes, the most important skill is knowing when to let go.

Many people accept the first offer because they're afraid the company will withdraw it. In reality, most employers expect some negotiation, as long as you're polite and realistic. Here's my advice. First, research the market so you know your value. Second, never give the first number if you can avoid it — ask what the budget for the role is. Third, if the salary is lower than you hoped, try negotiating other things: extra vacation days, a training budget, remote work. You might say: "I'm very excited about the role. I was hoping for something closer to X. If the salary isn't flexible, would it be possible to discuss other parts of the package?" And finally, once you've reached an agreement, ask for everything in writing.

In 1981, Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project published Getting to Yes, a book that changed how many people think about negotiation. Instead of seeing negotiation as a battle where one side wins and the other loses, they proposed a method called "principled negotiation". It has four main ideas. First, separate the people from the problem: you can be tough on the issue while being respectful to the person. Second, focus on interests, not positions. A position is what someone says they want ("I want a 20% raise"); an interest is why they want it ("I need to pay for my children's school"). When you understand interests, creative solutions often appear — perhaps a smaller raise plus an education allowance. Third, invent options for mutual gain before deciding. Finally, insist on objective criteria, such as market prices or expert standards, rather than pure willpower. The authors also introduced the concept of BATNA — your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. If you know what you'll do if the deal fails, you'll be much less likely to accept a bad one. Decades later, these ideas remain central to negotiation training around the world.

Surveys suggest that many professionals feel a large share of their meetings are unproductive. Why? In my experience, there are four main reasons. First, there's no clear purpose — people come without knowing what decision needs to be made. Second, the wrong people are invited: too many people, or not the ones who can actually decide. Third, nobody controls the discussion, so the conversation goes off track and the loudest voices dominate. And fourth — the most common — the meeting ends without clear action points. Everyone leaves thinking someone else will do the work. My rule is simple: no agenda, no meeting. And no meeting should end without three answers: what have we decided, who will do what, and by when.

In multinational companies, managers often notice a pattern: some team members — frequently non-native speakers — rarely speak up in meetings, even when they have excellent ideas. Research on international teams points to several reasons. One is language anxiety: the fear of making mistakes in front of colleagues, especially native speakers who talk quickly and use idioms. Another is cultural. In some cultures, interrupting is considered rude, and people wait for a pause that, in a fast-paced meeting, never comes. In others, junior employees are expected not to contradict senior ones publicly. The result is that companies lose valuable perspectives. Some organizations have started to change their meeting culture. Chairs are trained to invite quieter participants directly ("Marta, what's your view?"), agendas are shared in advance so people can prepare, and some meetings use a "round" format where everyone speaks in turn. Native speakers are encouraged to slow down and avoid slang. Non-native speakers, in turn, can benefit from learning a small set of phrases for entering a discussion. Ultimately, the goal is simple: the best idea should win — not the fastest speaker.

Journalism students are often taught a simple rule: when in doubt, use "said". The reason is that reporting verbs are never neutral. Imagine a politician who makes a statement about the economy. A newspaper could report that she "said", "claimed", "admitted", "insisted" or "boasted" that unemployment had fallen. Each verb sends a different message to the reader. "Claimed" suggests the statement might not be true; "admitted" suggests she was forced to reveal something; "boasted" implies arrogance. Researchers who study media bias have found that the choice of reporting verbs can influence how readers judge the people being quoted, even when the facts are identical. This is one reason why many style guides, such as those of major news agencies, recommend using neutral verbs like "said" in news reports and saving more expressive verbs for when they're clearly justified. As readers, we can protect ourselves by paying attention not only to what people are reported to have said, but also to the verbs journalists choose to report it. Sometimes, a single word tells you more about the writer than about the person being quoted.

For more than three centuries, the ship Nossa Senhora has been one of the great mysteries of the Brazilian coast. It is said to have sunk in a storm in 1712, carrying gold from the mines of Minas Gerais. The cargo is estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars today. For decades, treasure hunters have searched the area where the ship is believed to have gone down. Some local fishermen claim to have seen pieces of wood with Portuguese symbols after storms. However, historians are less certain. It is thought that the ship's records may have been exaggerated to impress the Portuguese king, and some researchers even believe the ship never existed. Whatever the truth, the legend is known to attract thousands of tourists to the region every year.

Every culture has its urban legends — stories that are passed from person to person and are widely believed to be true, despite little or no evidence. One well-known example is the idea that the Great Wall of China can be seen from space with the naked eye. It was widely repeated in textbooks for decades, but astronauts have said they could not see it. Another is the claim that we only use 10% of our brains, which is often attributed to early psychologists but has been rejected by neuroscientists: brain scans show activity across virtually all regions. In Brazil, many people grew up hearing that mixing mango and milk could be fatal. The belief is thought to have originated during the colonial period, possibly to stop enslaved workers on plantations from drinking the milk produced on the farms. Today, nutritionists confirm that the combination is perfectly safe. Why do such stories survive? Psychologists suggest that legends spread because they are simple, surprising and emotionally engaging — and because once a belief is shared by many people, questioning it feels strange. The lesson? "Everyone knows" is not the same as "it's true".

More than two thousand years ago, the Greek philosopher Aristotle described three ways to persuade an audience. Remarkably, his framework is still taught in business schools, law faculties and marketing courses today. The first is ethos: credibility. We're more likely to be persuaded by someone we trust or respect — which is why advertisers use doctors, athletes and celebrities, and why speakers often begin by explaining their experience. The second is pathos: emotion. Stories, images and music can make an audience feel joy, fear, anger or hope. It is pathos that makes a charity advert with a single child's face so much more powerful than a list of statistics. The third is logos: logic. This includes facts, data, examples and clear reasoning. What effective persuaders do is combine all three. A strong pitch might begin with a personal story (pathos), present data showing the size of the problem (logos), and mention the speaker's expertise or a respected partner (ethos). Remember three things tomorrow. First, structure. Judges can't give you points for arguments they can't follow, so signpost clearly: "My first point is...", "My second point is...". Second, engage with the other side. The worst thing you can do is read a prepared speech and ignore what your opponents have just said. Listen, take notes, and refute their strongest argument, not their weakest. Third, stay calm and respectful. Attacking your opponent personally is a fallacy, and judges will penalize you for it. And one more thing: it's perfectly fine to concede a point. Saying "Admittedly, that's true, but..." shows confidence, not weakness. The best debaters aren't the loudest — they're the clearest.

In recent years, the idea of a four-day working week — with no reduction in pay — has moved from the fringes to the mainstream. Supporters argue that it improves employees' well-being, reduces burnout and can even increase productivity. They point to a large trial in the United Kingdom in 2022, coordinated by the non-profit 4 Day Week Global with researchers from several universities, in which around 60 companies reduced working hours. According to the organizers, the large majority of participating companies chose to continue with the policy after the trial, and many employees reported lower stress and better sleep. Similar pilots have been carried out in countries such as Iceland, Spain and, more recently, Brazil. Critics, however, raise several concerns. Admittedly, the results look impressive, but the companies that volunteered for trials may not be representative: they were probably already open to flexible work. Furthermore, a four-day week may be much harder to implement in sectors like healthcare, education or retail, where someone must be present at all times. Some economists also question whether productivity gains can be sustained in the long term. On balance, the evidence so far suggests that the four-day week can work well in some contexts — but it is unlikely to be a universal solution.

Historians are often cautious about "counterfactual" questions — imagining what would have happened if events had been different — but these questions can help us understand how fragile history really is. Consider the discovery of penicillin. In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday to find that mould had contaminated one of his bacterial cultures — and that the bacteria around the mould had died. If he had cleaned his laboratory before leaving, or if the mould had landed on a different plate, he might never have noticed the effect. Penicillin, and the antibiotics that followed, have since saved millions of lives. Or take the Post-it note, which we saw in an earlier unit: if Spencer Silver hadn't "failed" to make a strong glue, one of the world's most famous office products would not have been invented. Of course, history is rarely shaped by a single moment. Had Fleming not noticed the mould, someone else might eventually have discovered penicillin. Still, these stories remind us that chance, curiosity and the ability to notice the unexpected have played a much larger role in human progress than we usually admit.

"Two roads diverged in a wood, and I — / I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference." These lines from Robert Frost's 1916 poem "The Road Not Taken" are among the most quoted in American literature, often printed on posters encouraging people to be brave and different. Yet many literary critics argue that the poem is widely misunderstood. Earlier in the poem, Frost actually describes the two roads as being worn "really about the same". The traveller only imagines that, years later, he will tell the story as if his choice had been dramatic and meaningful. In other words, the poem may be less about bravery and more about how we construct stories about our decisions after the fact. Psychologists have found something similar: we tend to justify our choices once they are made, convincing ourselves that the path we took was the right one. If we had chosen differently, we would probably be just as good at explaining why that choice was the best. Perhaps that's not a bad thing. If we didn't have this ability, we might spend our lives tormented by the roads we didn't take.

Australian palliative care nurse Bronnie Ware spent years caring for people in the last weeks of their lives, and she wrote about the regrets they shared with her. Her list became famous around the world. Many of her patients said: "I wish I'd had the courage to live a life true to myself, not the life others expected of me." Others said: "I wish I hadn't worked so hard." Some told her: "I wish I'd had the courage to express my feelings," and "I wish I had stayed in touch with my friends." And finally: "I wish I had let myself be happier." What's striking is that none of these regrets is about money or possessions. They're all about courage, relationships and choices — things we can still change today.

Regret has a bad reputation. We're often told to "live with no regrets" and to avoid dwelling on the past. But some psychologists argue that regret, when handled well, is one of our most useful emotions. In his book The Power of Regret, Daniel Pink describes a large survey in which thousands of people around the world shared their regrets. He identified four core types: foundation regrets ("If only I'd saved more money / looked after my health"), boldness regrets ("I wish I'd asked her out / started that business"), moral regrets ("I wish I hadn't cheated / been unkind") and connection regrets ("I wish I had kept in touch with my brother"). Interestingly, regrets about inaction — the chances we didn't take — tend to last longer than regrets about actions. Pink suggests a three-step method for using regret productively. First, reframe it: talk about it or write it down, which reduces its emotional power. Second, be kind to yourself — treat your past self as you would treat a friend who made a mistake. Third, extract a lesson for the future: "Next time, I'll speak up." Regret, in this view, isn't something to avoid. It's information about what we value most.

In the early 1970s, the oil company Shell began using a technique called scenario planning. Instead of trying to predict a single future, its planners imagined several possible futures and asked: "Suppose this happened — how would we respond?" One of the scenarios they explored was a sudden, dramatic rise in oil prices. Most companies considered this unlikely. When the oil crisis of 1973 arrived, Shell was widely seen as being better prepared than many of its competitors, and the company's approach became famous in business schools. Today, scenario planning is used by governments, cities and businesses around the world. The idea is not to guess correctly, but to become more flexible. A city might ask: "What if sea levels rose faster than expected?" or "Supposing a pandemic closed schools for months, how would children learn?" The process often reveals weaknesses that nobody had noticed. Psychologists point out that individuals can benefit from the same thinking. Imagining a worst-case scenario — and planning how you would cope — can actually reduce anxiety, because the future feels less threatening once you have a plan. As the old saying goes: hope for the best, but prepare for the worst.

It's Sunday morning on one of the busiest avenues in the city — except that today, there isn't a single car. Since the avenue started closing to traffic on Sundays, it has become a huge open-air park, which attracts thousands of cyclists, skaters, families and street musicians. Bogotá, in Colombia, is often cited as the pioneer of this idea: its weekly Ciclovía, which began in the 1970s, now opens many kilometres of roads to people instead of cars. Not everyone is happy, of course. Some shop owners, most of whom depend on drivers, complain that they lose customers. But surveys in several cities suggest that most residents support the idea, many of whom say it's the only time they feel the city really belongs to them.

Imagine a neighbourhood in which you could reach almost everything you need — work, school, shops, a doctor, a park — within a 15-minute walk or bike ride. This is the idea behind the "15-minute city", a concept popularized by the urbanist Carlos Moreno, whose work influenced the plans of Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo. Supporters argue that cities designed around cars have created long commutes, pollution and lonely suburbs, all of which damage our health and quality of life. By bringing services closer to people, the 15-minute city aims to cut emissions, revive local businesses and give residents more free time. Several cities, among which are Melbourne, Barcelona and Bogotá, have experimented with similar ideas. The concept is not without its critics, however. Some point out that in many cities, including those in Brazil, jobs and good services are concentrated in a few central areas, which means that a 15-minute city could easily become a privilege for the rich. Others fear that improving a neighbourhood will push up rents, forcing out the very people for whom the changes were intended. The challenge, then, is not only to design better neighbourhoods, but to ensure that everyone can afford to live in them.

Brazil is undergoing one of the fastest demographic transitions in the world. Having had one of the youngest populations in the 1970s, the country is now ageing rapidly. Two trends explain this. First, the birth rate has fallen dramatically: Brazilian women today have, on average, fewer than two children, compared with around six in the 1960s. Second, life expectancy has increased considerably, thanks to better healthcare and sanitation. The result is a population growing older faster than in many European countries, which took much longer to go through the same change. Faced with this situation, the country will need to rethink its pension system, its healthcare services and even the way its cities are designed. Having said that, an older population also brings opportunities, from new businesses to a more experienced workforce.

Before 2020, remote work was a privilege enjoyed by a small minority of workers. Then, almost overnight, the COVID-19 pandemic forced millions of office employees to work from their kitchens and living rooms. Having been told for years that remote work was impossible, many companies discovered that it worked surprisingly well. Freed from long commutes, employees gained hours of free time each week. Some left expensive capital cities altogether, moving to smaller towns or the coast and taking their salaries with them. Several countries, including Portugal and Costa Rica, began offering special visas designed to attract "digital nomads". Not everyone has benefited equally, however. Jobs requiring physical presence — in hospitals, shops, factories and construction — cannot be done from home, which means that remote work has, in some ways, increased the gap between different groups of workers. Managers, too, have expressed concerns, arguing that teams working only online lose creativity and that young employees miss out on learning from experienced colleagues. Having experimented with every possible model, many organizations have now settled on a hybrid approach. Having said that, the debate is far from over.

When people hear that most Brazilians are now online, they often assume the digital divide has disappeared. However, the reality is more complex. Although the majority of the population uses the internet, many low-income users rely only on a mobile phone with a limited data plan, whereas wealthier families usually have fast broadband and several devices at home. This difference matters. Doing homework, applying for a job or taking an online course on a small phone screen is much harder. During the pandemic, when classes moved online, many children were left behind despite their schools' efforts. Nevertheless, there is some good news: public Wi-Fi programmes and community centres are helping to narrow the gap. Connection is no longer the only issue, though. Digital skills are just as important.

Artificial intelligence has been described as the most important technology of our time. Yet economists disagree sharply about whether it will reduce or increase inequality. On the one hand, optimists argue that AI tools could empower people who have traditionally been left behind. A small farmer can now get advice about crops in her own language, while a student without access to private tutors can ask a chatbot to explain a difficult maths problem. Although these tools are not perfect, they are often free or cheap. On the other hand, pessimists point out that previous waves of technology tended to benefit those who already had capital and education. Despite creating new jobs, automation has often replaced routine tasks performed by lower-paid workers, whereas highly skilled professionals have seen their productivity — and salaries — increase. There is also the question of who owns the technology: a handful of large companies, most of which are based in the United States and China. In spite of these concerns, most experts agree on one point: the outcome is not inevitable. Whether AI narrows or widens the gap will depend largely on political choices, including investment in education, regulation and public access to digital tools.

Many students think the most important thing in an essay is grammar. In fact, in the Cambridge B2 First, your writing is assessed on four criteria. First, content: have you answered the question and included all the required points? Second, communicative achievement: is the style appropriate — formal, in the case of an essay — and does your text hold the reader's attention? Third, organization: are your ideas logically connected, with clear paragraphs and a good variety of linking words? And finally, language: how wide and accurate is your vocabulary and grammar? So, as you can see, grammar is only one part. A text with a few small mistakes but excellent organization will often score better than a perfect text that doesn't answer the question. My advice? Spend five minutes planning before you write. It makes a huge difference.

In many countries, including Brazil, the cost of higher education is a controversial issue. While public universities offer free courses, places are limited and highly competitive. This essay will consider whether university education should be free for everyone.. . There are strong arguments in favour of free higher education. Firstly, it can increase social mobility. When students do not have to pay fees, talented young people from low-income families have a real chance of entering professions such as medicine or engineering. Furthermore, a more educated population tends to benefit the whole economy, as graduates generally earn more and contribute more in taxes.. . On the other hand, it could be argued that free education is not truly free, since it is paid for by all taxpayers, including those who never go to university. In addition, if universities receive too little funding, the quality of teaching may suffer. As a result, some experts suggest alternatives, such as income-based loans, where graduates repay their fees only when they earn above a certain salary.. . In conclusion, all things considered, I believe that higher education should remain free at public universities, as it is one of the most effective ways of reducing inequality. However, governments must ensure that it is adequately funded and that access is fair for students from all backgrounds.

Here's an exercise I often suggest. For two weeks, write down every worry you have — "I might lose my job", "My presentation will be a disaster" — and then check later whether it actually happened. In a small study at Penn State University, researchers asked people with generalized anxiety to do something similar. They found that most of the participants' worries did not come true, and when something negative did happen, people often coped better than they had expected. In other words, they needn't have worried so much. Of course, this doesn't mean all worry is useless. Some concern helps us prepare. But if you look back at your list and see that you spent hours worrying about things that never happened, it can be a real wake-up call. You might decide to save your energy for the problems that actually appear.

History is full of people whose failures turned out to be blessings in disguise. Take the author J.K. Rowling, who has said in interviews that her manuscript for the first Harry Potter book was rejected by many publishers before Bloomsbury accepted it. Any one of those editors could have changed literary history; they simply didn't. Steve Jobs, forced out of Apple in 1985, later described being fired as one of the best things that could have happened to him, because it freed him to start again. Of course, survivor stories like these can be misleading. For every person whose rejection led to success, there are many others who might have been equally talented but never got a second chance. Psychologist Richard Wiseman, who studied people who considered themselves lucky or unlucky, suggested that "lucky" people tend to notice opportunities, listen to their intuition and recover quickly from bad experiences. In one of his well-known experiments, participants were asked to count the photographs in a newspaper. Many of the "unlucky" ones missed a large message inside it telling them they needn't have kept counting. Perhaps luck is partly a matter of where we choose to look.

Most of us think we're good listeners. But research on communication suggests that we often listen in order to reply, not to understand. While the other person is talking, we're planning what to say next. Active listening is different. It means giving the person your full attention, avoiding being distracted by your phone, and trying not to interrupt. It also means checking that you've understood: "So what you're saying is..." People who are listened to in this way feel respected. They're more likely to trust you, and less likely to feel misunderstood. A simple exercise: in your next conversation, try waiting two seconds before you reply. You'll be surprised how much more you notice — including what's said between the lines.

Being understood is one of our deepest psychological needs. Researchers studying relationships have found that people who feel understood by their partners tend to report higher satisfaction, and in some studies even smaller increases in stress during conflict. Interestingly, it seems that what matters most is not having our ideas accepted, but being listened to. In one line of research, participants who were allowed to explain their point of view — even when the other person disagreed — reported feeling more respected than those who were simply agreed with quickly. Feeling misunderstood, on the other hand, can be painful. Many people describe being left out or not being taken seriously at work as one of the most frustrating experiences of their professional lives. Psychologists suggest a few habits for helping others feel understood: asking open questions, repeating key points in your own words and avoiding being too quick to give advice. Admitting to having made assumptions also helps: "I think I misunderstood you — can you explain again?" Sometimes, the most powerful thing we can do is not to have the right answer, but to have truly listened.

Today we're comparing idioms from different languages. Let's start with rain. In English, when it's raining heavily, people sometimes say "it's raining cats and dogs" — though, honestly, most people just say "it's pouring". In Brazilian Portuguese, it's "raining pocket knives".

I love that one! And when something is very expensive, English speakers say it "costs an arm and a leg", whereas Brazilians say it "costs the eyes of the face". Same idea — very valuable parts of the body!
Exactly. And some idioms are almost identical. "Break the ice" exists in English, Portuguese and many other languages.
