For most of the twentieth century, language teaching focused on two things: grammar rules and individual words. But in the 1990s, the linguist Michael Lewis proposed what he called the "Lexical Approach". His central idea was simple but powerful: language is not made of grammar and words, but largely of "chunks" — groups of words that native speakers store and use as single units. Phrases like "by the way", "I'm not sure", "make a decision" or "as far as I know" are not built word by word each time we speak; they come ready-made. Corpus research — the study of very large collections of real texts — supports this view, showing that a large part of everyday language consists of recurring combinations. This helps explain why learners can know thousands of words and still sound unnatural: they combine words in ways that are grammatically correct but that native speakers simply don't use, like "do a decision" or "strong rain". It also explains why fluent speakers can talk so quickly: they don't need to build every sentence from scratch. For learners, the practical lesson is clear. When you meet a new word, don't just learn its translation. Notice the words around it, write down the whole chunk, and practise it until it comes out automatically.

According to the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR), a B2 user is an "independent user" who can understand the main ideas of complex texts, interact with native speakers with a degree of fluency and spontaneity, and produce clear, detailed texts on a wide range of subjects. In practical terms, this is a significant milestone. Many universities around the world accept B2 as a minimum level of English for some courses, and many international employers consider it the point at which someone can work effectively in English. However, reaching B2 does not mean that you will understand everything. You may still struggle with fast speech, strong regional accents, jokes and cultural references. You will continue to make mistakes — but, crucially, they will rarely prevent communication, and you will often be able to notice and correct them yourself. Perhaps the most important change is psychological. At B2, English stops being only a subject that you study and becomes a tool that you use: to read the news, watch series without subtitles, follow a TED talk or argue your point in a meeting. From here, progress depends less on courses and more on exposure. The more you read, listen and speak, the closer you will get to C1 — and, more importantly, the richer your life in English will become.

Psychologists who study what they call "narrative identity" argue that we don't just have experiences — we turn them into stories, and those stories become who we are. The researcher Dan McAdams has spent decades studying these life stories. One pattern that comes up again and again is what he calls a "redemption sequence": a story in which something bad turns into something good. "I lost my job, but it led me to find my real calling." Research in this area suggests that people who tell their lives this way tend to report higher well-being. Now, I'm not saying we should invent happy endings. But it's worth asking: what story are you telling about yourself? And is it the only possible version? Because, as it turns out, we have more freedom to rewrite it than we usually think.

Ask people whether their personality will change much over the next ten years and most will say no. Ask them how much it has changed over the past ten years, however, and they will readily admit that it has changed considerably. Psychologists Jordi Quoidbach, Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson called this the "end of history illusion": at every age, we seem to believe that the person we are today is, more or less, the finished product. Their study, published in Science in 2013, surveyed thousands of adults and found that people consistently underestimated how much their values, preferences and personalities would change in the future. The illusion has practical consequences. Because we assume our current tastes will last, we may pay too much today for things our future selves won't value — a tattoo, say, or a ticket to see a favourite band a decade from now. Longitudinal research on personality offers a more nuanced picture still. Traits such as conscientiousness and emotional stability tend to increase gradually throughout adulthood, a pattern sometimes described as "maturation". None of this means that we are endlessly changeable; there is real continuity in who we are. But it does suggest that the question "Who am I?" is better answered in pencil than in ink. The self, it seems, is less a statue than a river.

Does the language you speak change the way you think? For much of the twentieth century, the strong version of this idea — that language determines thought — was largely rejected. But a weaker version has gained support. The cognitive scientist Lera Boroditsky and others have studied, for instance, an Aboriginal community in Australia, the Kuuk Thaayorre, whose language uses cardinal directions — north, south, east, west — instead of "left" and "right". Speakers have been reported to stay remarkably well oriented, even indoors. Other studies have looked at colour: Russian has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, and some experiments found that Russian speakers were slightly faster at distinguishing those shades. Does this mean we're prisoners of our language? Most researchers would say not. But it does suggest that each language trains our attention in particular ways — and that learning another one can show us the world from a slightly different angle.

Every translator faces the same impossible choice: be faithful to the words or to the meaning. Translate too literally, and the result may be accurate but lifeless; translate too freely, and you risk replacing the author's voice with your own. Nowhere is this clearer than with humour, poetry and culturally loaded words. Take the Portuguese "jeitinho". A dictionary might offer "knack" or "way around something", but neither conveys the mixture of creativity, flexibility and occasional rule-bending the word suggests to Brazilians. A translator can choose to keep the original word and explain it, to find an approximate equivalent, or to rewrite the sentence entirely. Each option gains something and loses something. Machine translation has transformed the field in recent years. For everyday texts — instructions, emails, the gist of a news article — modern tools are remarkably good, and many professional translators now use them as a first draft. Literary translation, however, remains a stubbornly human craft. A novel's rhythm, ambiguity and wordplay depend on choices that require an understanding not only of two languages but of two cultures. Perhaps the best definition of a good translation is one that makes the reader forget it is one. If so, the translator's greatest achievement is to become invisible — which may explain why so few readers can name the translators of their favourite books.

The term "third culture kids" was coined in the 1950s by the American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem, who studied children of families living abroad. The idea is that these children grow up between their parents' culture and the culture of the country where they live, and end up creating a third culture of their own. Ask one of them "Where are you from?" and you may get a long pause. Many describe a feeling of belonging everywhere and nowhere. Strange as it may seem, they often feel most at home with other third culture kids, regardless of nationality. There are clear advantages: adaptability, language skills, an ability to see situations from several perspectives. But there are challenges too. Repeated goodbyes can make some people reluctant to form deep attachments. So common is this experience that many international schools now run programmes to help students deal with transitions.

Much as we talk about home as a place, researchers who study belonging suggest it is better understood as a set of relationships. In one influential framework, environmental psychologists describe "place attachment" as developing through three overlapping dimensions: the people we share a place with, the meaningful experiences we have there, and the physical features we come to know intimately — the smell of a particular bakery, the sound of the street at dawn. This helps explain a phenomenon that puzzles many migrants. Returning to their hometown after years away, they find the streets unchanged but the feeling gone. Their friends have moved on, the rhythms of daily life have changed, and they themselves are no longer the same people. Home, it turns out, does not stay where we left it. Brazil offers a vivid illustration. Over the twentieth century, millions of people moved from the countryside and the Northeast to cities in the Southeast. Many of them recreated home in their new neighbourhoods through food, music and festivals: the forró halls and Northeastern fairs of São Paulo are a direct result of this. Such was the scale of the movement that it transformed the culture of the cities that received it. Perhaps the lesson is that belonging is not something we find but something we build. Small as they are, the daily rituals of a place — a greeting from a neighbour, a familiar route to work — slowly turn a city into home.

Small talk has a pretty bad reputation. People call it shallow, fake, a waste of time. But, as it happens, research suggests otherwise. In one well-known study, the psychologists Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn asked people to have a brief, friendly exchange with a barista instead of just ordering and leaving. Those who chatted reported a better mood and a greater sense of belonging. Sandstrom has also found that our interactions with so-called "weak ties" — the neighbour, the bus driver, the person at the gym — contribute to our happiness more than we tend to assume. Mind you, I'm not saying you should corner strangers and talk about the weather for half an hour. But a two-minute chat is sort of like social glue. It's how relationships start. Come to think of it, most of my close friends began as people I made small talk with.

In 1973, the sociologist Mark Granovetter published a paper with a deliberately paradoxical title: "The Strength of Weak Ties". Studying how people in a Boston suburb had found their jobs, he noticed something surprising. Many had heard about the opportunity not from close friends but from acquaintances — people they saw only occasionally. His explanation was elegant. Our close friends tend to move in the same circles we do, so they mostly know what we already know. Acquaintances, by contrast, connect us to different networks and therefore to new information. The idea has since become one of the most cited in the social sciences, and recent research has largely supported it. A large study of LinkedIn users, published in Science in 2022, found that moderately weak ties were the most useful for job mobility. That said, weak ties do more than help us find work. They also seem to matter for our well-being. A quick chat with a neighbour or a familiar face at the market can make a city feel friendlier and less anonymous. Perhaps this is why so many people felt strangely lonely during the pandemic lockdowns, even when they kept in touch with close friends online: what had disappeared were the small, casual encounters that once filled their days. Small talk, it seems, is not so small after all.

In 1997, the Harvard professor Clayton Christensen published The Innovator's Dilemma, a book that changed how business leaders think about innovation. His central question was a puzzling one: why do successful, well-managed companies fail? His answer was that they often fail precisely because they do the right things — they listen to their best customers and focus on improving their most profitable products. Meanwhile, a new technology appears at the bottom of the market. At first, it's cheaper, simpler and, frankly, worse. Established firms ignore it, because their best customers don't want it. But the new technology improves, and by the time it's good enough for mainstream customers, it's too late. Not only have the newcomers taken the low end of the market; they've learned how to move up. Kodak is often cited as an example: one of its own engineers built an early digital camera in 1975, yet the company struggled to embrace the technology that eventually helped to bring it down.

For decades, opening a bank account in Brazil was, for many people, a frustrating experience. Fees were high, branches were crowded and the paperwork seemed endless. Large numbers of adults, particularly among lower-income groups, had no account at all. Then, in the 2010s, a wave of digital banks began to change the picture. Offering free accounts and credit cards that could be managed entirely through an app, companies such as Nubank attracted millions of customers who had long been ignored or poorly served by traditional institutions. Never before had so many Brazilians been able to open an account in a matter of minutes, from their phones. The traditional banks, at first, appeared unconcerned. Only when the new players had gathered tens of millions of customers did several of them respond seriously, launching their own digital brands and cutting fees. The changes did not stop there. In 2020, the Central Bank launched Pix, an instant payment system that is free for individuals. Not only did Pix make transfers immediate, but it also allowed small businesses and informal workers to accept payments without expensive card machines. Its adoption was remarkably fast: within a few years it had become one of the most widely used payment methods in the country. Seldom has a public innovation been embraced so quickly. Experts still debate the risks, from fraud to rising household debt. Yet few would deny that, in little more than a decade, the relationship between Brazilians and their money has been transformed.

One of the most talked-about experiments in the world of work in recent years has been the four-day week. In 2022, a large pilot programme in the UK involved around sixty companies, whose employees moved to a four-day week with no loss of pay, on the condition that productivity was maintained. The results, published in 2023, attracted international attention. Most of the participating companies said they would continue with the new schedule. Researchers reported reductions in stress and burnout among employees, as well as improvements in sleep and work-life balance. Similar trials have since been carried out in other countries, including Brazil. Critics point out, however, that the companies involved chose to take part, which may have influenced the results, and that the model is far harder to implement in sectors such as healthcare or retail. The debate, in other words, is far from over.

The expansion of app-based work has been one of the most significant changes in the labour market of the past decade. In Brazil, as in many other countries, the growth of ride-hailing and food delivery platforms has created opportunities for hundreds of thousands of people, particularly during periods of high unemployment. For many workers, the attraction lies in the flexibility these platforms offer: the ability to choose when and how long to work, and the absence of a boss in the traditional sense. However, this flexibility comes at a price. Unlike conventional employees, most platform workers do not have access to paid holidays, sick pay or guaranteed minimum earnings. Their income depends on fluctuations in demand and on decisions made by algorithms over which they have little control or understanding. The suspension of an account, for example, can mean the immediate loss of a worker's livelihood, often without a clear explanation. These concerns have led to growing pressure for regulation. Governments in several countries, including Brazil, have attempted to introduce rules guaranteeing minimum standards of pay and social protection, though such proposals have frequently met with resistance from both companies and some workers, who fear the loss of flexibility. The challenge for policymakers, therefore, lies in the development of a model that combines the advantages of flexibility with an adequate level of security. The outcome of this debate will have a profound impact not only on platform workers, but on the future of work as a whole.

A few years ago, Google ran an internal research project, known as Project Aristotle, to find out why some of its teams performed better than others. You'd think the answer would be about talent — put the smartest people together and you're bound to succeed. But that's not what they found. According to the company's own summary, the most important factor was psychological safety: whether team members feel safe to take risks, ask questions and admit mistakes without being embarrassed or punished. The concept was developed by Amy Edmondson, a professor at Harvard Business School. Her early research in hospitals produced a surprising result: the better teams appeared to report more errors — not because they made more, she concluded, but because people felt safe enough to talk about them. So, if you're a leader, the message is clear. Your team may well be hiding problems from you. And if they are, you might as well be flying blind.

For much of the twentieth century, the ideal leader was imagined as a confident, decisive figure who had all the answers. That image may well be changing. A growing body of research suggests that some of the most effective leaders combine ambition with a quality that is rarely associated with power: humility. In his influential study of companies that had made the leap from good to great performance, the management writer Jim Collins described what he called "Level 5 leaders" — executives who blended intense professional will with personal modesty. They were quick to give credit to others for success and to take responsibility for failure. Later studies have pointed in a similar direction, linking humble leadership with greater team engagement and learning. Why should humility matter so much? One explanation is that no leader, however talented, can possibly know everything in a complex organization. Leaders who admit what they don't know are more likely to ask for input, and their teams are more likely to offer it. Arrogant leaders, by contrast, are bound to hear only what they want to hear. None of this means that leaders should be passive or indecisive. Teams still need direction, and there will be moments when someone simply has to decide. But the old idea that admitting a mistake is a sign of weakness looks increasingly outdated. You'd think, after decades of evidence, that this lesson would be widely accepted. In many workplaces, however, it is still waiting to be learned.

More than two thousand years ago, Aristotle argued that persuasion rests on three pillars: ethos, your credibility; pathos, the emotions you create; and logos, your logic and evidence. Notice, by the way, that even his theory comes in three parts. The rule of three is everywhere in rhetoric. Julius Caesar's famous message, often quoted as "veni, vidi, vici" — "I came, I saw, I conquered" — is perhaps the most famous example. Why does it work? Psychologists suggest that three is the smallest number that creates a pattern. Two items feel like a comparison; four start to feel like a list. Three feels complete. The second trick is antithesis — putting opposites side by side. Think of Neil Armstrong's line about "one small step for man" and "one giant leap for mankind". And the third is the rhetorical question, which turns a lecture into a conversation. So, what do these techniques have in common? They make your message easier to remember. And in a pitch, what matters most is what people remember after you've left the room.

Every year, thousands of founders stand in front of investors hoping to secure funding. Most of them fail — and, according to experienced investors, the reason is rarely the idea itself. What sinks most pitches is the way the idea is communicated. The first mistake is starting in the wrong place. Many founders open with their company history or a detailed description of their technology. Investors, however, want to understand the problem before they care about the solution. A strong pitch begins with a pain point the audience can feel — ideally one that is large, urgent and growing. The second mistake is trying to say too much. Faced with a short time slot, nervous presenters often try to cram every feature onto their slides. The result is confusion. What investors remember is a single clear message: who the product is for, what it does, and why it is better than the alternatives. The third mistake is neglecting evidence. Enthusiasm is necessary, but it is not sufficient. Investors want to see traction — paying customers, growth rates, partnerships — that proves the idea works outside the founder's imagination. Finally, many pitches simply end. The speaker reaches the last slide, says "thank you" and waits for questions. A compelling pitch, by contrast, finishes with a clear call to action: what the founder is asking for and what the investor will gain. The best founders understand that a pitch is not a lecture. It is the beginning of a relationship. And, as with any relationship, first impressions matter enormously.

When people think of great scientific discoveries, Brazil isn't always the first country that comes to mind. Yet Brazilian scientists have made important contributions. In 1909, the physician Carlos Chagas described a new disease — now known as Chagas disease — identifying the parasite that causes it, the insect that transmits it and its clinical symptoms, an achievement that is often described as unique in the history of medicine. The country has also been praised for its agricultural research: Embrapa, the public agricultural research company founded in the 1970s, is widely credited with helping to transform the tropical savannah of the Cerrado into productive farmland — though the environmental costs of that transformation are still debated. And during the Zika outbreak of 2015 and 2016, Brazilian researchers were among the first to establish the link between the virus and microcephaly in newborns. These achievements could not have been made without public funding, which is why cuts to research budgets are a constant concern for the scientific community.

For decades, the Hungarian-born biochemist Katalin Karikó was considered, by many of her colleagues, to be chasing an impossible dream. Her idea was to use messenger RNA — the molecule that carries genetic instructions inside cells — to make the body produce its own proteins, which could then be used to treat or prevent disease. The problem was that synthetic mRNA, when injected into animals, triggered a strong inflammatory reaction. Grant applications were rejected repeatedly, and in the 1990s she was demoted at the University of Pennsylvania. Most researchers would have given up. Karikó did not. In the early 2000s, working with the immunologist Drew Weissman, she discovered that the inflammatory reaction could be largely avoided if one of the building blocks of the mRNA was slightly modified. Their paper, published in 2005, attracted little attention at the time. Fifteen years later, it was fundamental to one of the fastest medical responses in history. When the COVID-19 pandemic struck, vaccines based on modified mRNA were developed, tested and approved in less than a year — a process that had traditionally taken a decade or more. Hundreds of millions of doses were administered worldwide. In 2023, Karikó and Weissman were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Her story is often told as a lesson in persistence. But it also raises uncomfortable questions about the way science is funded. How many other good ideas have been abandoned because they could not be explained in a short grant proposal, or did not produce quick results?

In November 2018, the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced that he had used the gene-editing tool CRISPR to alter the DNA of human embryos, resulting in the birth of twin girls. His stated aim was to make them resistant to HIV. The reaction from the scientific community was almost universally negative. Critics argued that the procedure was medically unnecessary, that its long-term effects were unknown, and that the changes could be passed on to future generations. Many questioned whether the parents had given truly informed consent. He was later sentenced to prison in China. The case led to calls from leading scientists that a global moratorium be placed on heritable genome editing until its safety and ethics could be properly assessed. It's worth noting that gene editing in non-reproductive cells — which only affects the patient — is a different matter, and therapies of this kind have already been approved in some countries. The line, most experts agree, is crossed when changes are made that will be inherited.

The line, most experts agree, is crossed when changes are made that will be inherited.

Few technologies have raised hopes and fears as dramatically as gene editing. Tools such as CRISPR, whose developers Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020, allow scientists to modify DNA with a precision that would have been unimaginable a generation ago. The potential benefits are enormous. Inherited diseases that have caused suffering for centuries could, in theory, be corrected. In 2023, regulators in the United Kingdom and the United States approved the first therapy based on CRISPR, designed to treat sickle cell disease. Yet the same technology raises profound ethical questions. If it becomes possible to eliminate a disease, should it also be possible to select for height, intelligence or appearance? Critics warn of a slippery slope towards "designer babies" and a world in which genetic advantages are available only to the wealthy. Disability rights advocates have also asked who gets to decide which human traits count as "defects". Most scientific bodies currently insist that a clear distinction be maintained between somatic editing, which affects only the individual patient, and germline editing, whose changes would be inherited by future generations. The first is increasingly accepted; the second remains, in most countries, prohibited. But laws vary from one country to another, and technology tends to move faster than regulation. Were it not for international cooperation, the rules could easily be bypassed by researchers moving to countries with weaker oversight. Perhaps the most important question is not what science can do, but who should decide what it ought to do — scientists, governments, patients or society as a whole. Be that as it may, it seems essential that these decisions not be left to a few laboratories alone.

Overall, cycling increased dramatically over the period, although there were some fluctuations. In 2010, there were roughly 20,000 daily trips. This figure remained fairly stable until 2014, when the city opened its first network of cycle lanes. Over the following four years, the number of trips more than doubled, reaching just over 45,000 in 2018. There was a sharp fall in 2020, when trips plummeted to around 25,000, which would appear to be linked to lockdown restrictions. However, the figure recovered rapidly, peaking at approximately 60,000 in 2023 — a threefold increase compared with 2010 — before levelling off. Notice what I did there: an overview first, then the key figures, and a careful "would appear to be linked" — because the graph alone can't prove the cause.

In 1954, the American writer Darrell Huff published a small book with a provocative title: How to Lie with Statistics. Despite its age, many of its warnings remain remarkably relevant. Perhaps the most common trap is confusing correlation with causation. Countries that consume more chocolate per person, for example, tend to have won more Nobel Prizes per capita — a correlation highlighted, half-jokingly, in a 2012 article in a medical journal. Few would seriously conclude that chocolate makes people smarter. A far more likely explanation is that both are associated with a third factor: national wealth. Yet similar reasoning appears regularly in headlines about diet, technology and health. A second trap involves relative and absolute risk. A headline announcing that a medicine "doubles the risk" of a side effect sounds alarming. But if the risk rises from one in 10,000 to two in 10,000, the absolute increase is tiny. Both statements are technically true; only one gives the reader a fair picture. Third, there is the problem of the sample. A survey of 200 enthusiastic app users cannot tell us much about the population as a whole, however impressive its results may appear. Finally, graphs themselves can mislead. By starting the vertical axis at a number other than zero, a designer can make a marginal change look dramatic. None of this means that statistics are useless — quite the opposite. Used carefully, they are among the most powerful tools we have for understanding the world. The point is that numbers, like words, need to be read critically. As a rule of thumb, it would seem wise to ask three questions of any statistic: compared to what, measured how, and according to whom?

In 2016, researchers at MIT launched an online experiment called the Moral Machine. It presented visitors with variations of the famous trolley problem, adapted for self-driving cars: should the car save its passengers or the pedestrians? The young or the elderly? More lives or fewer? Millions of people from over two hundred countries and territories took part, and the results were published in Nature in 2018. Some preferences were broadly shared: in general, people chose to spare more lives rather than fewer, humans rather than animals, and the young rather than the old. But there were also notable cultural differences. Participants from some regions, for example, showed a weaker preference for sparing younger people. Whatever you think of the method — and it has been criticized for oversimplifying real situations — the study raises a difficult question. However universal our moral instincts may seem, they may not be the same everywhere. So whose values should a machine follow?

Few moral questions are as old, or as practical, as this one. The eighteenth-century philosopher Immanuel Kant took an uncompromising position. Lying, he argued, is always wrong, whatever the consequences — even, in a much-debated example, when a murderer comes to your door asking where your friend is hiding. However extreme this may sound, Kant's reasoning was that a lie treats other people as mere instruments and undermines the trust on which all communication depends. Most people find this conclusion hard to accept. Admittedly, honesty is a value almost every culture shares. Even so, few of us believe we should tell a friend that their wedding speech was boring, or tell a terrified patient every grim statistic at once. Consequentialist philosophers, following thinkers such as John Stuart Mill, argue that the morality of an action depends on its outcomes. If a lie prevents serious harm, it may be not only permissible but right. Yet this view has its own difficulties. Who decides which consequences matter, and how far ahead must we look? A "white lie" that spares someone's feelings today may damage their trust tomorrow. Psychologists add an interesting twist. Research suggests that most of us lie more often than we think, and that we tend to judge our own lies far more generously than those of others. Much as we may admire honesty in principle, our everyday behaviour is more complicated. Perhaps the most realistic answer is that honesty is a strong default, not an absolute rule. Granted, that leaves us with grey areas. But moral life, whatever philosophers may wish, has always been full of them.

Why do stories grip us so powerfully? Part of the answer may lie in the brain. When we read a list of facts, the areas involved in processing language become active. But a number of studies have suggested that vivid descriptions can engage other areas too. In one experiment, words with strong smell associations, like "coffee" or "perfume", appeared to activate regions linked to the sense of smell. Metaphors involving texture — "a rough day", "a velvety voice" — seemed to engage areas related to touch. Researchers are cautious about these findings, and brain-imaging studies are notoriously difficult to interpret. But they're consistent with something writers have always known: a well-told story isn't just understood, it's experienced. That's also why stories are remembered so much better than statistics. Tell people that thousands of children are hungry, and they nod. Tell them about one child — her name, her face, what she had for breakfast — and they act.

"For sale: baby shoes, never worn." These six words are often described as the shortest story ever written, and they are frequently attributed to Ernest Hemingway, who is said to have written them to win a bet. There is, however, no reliable evidence that he did; similar newspaper adverts had appeared years before. Whoever wrote it, the story is a perfect illustration of a principle at the heart of good writing: what is left out can be as powerful as what is put in. The reader is never told what happened. There is no description of grief, no explanation, no ending. And yet most readers feel a sudden, heart-breaking weight. The story works precisely because the reader's imagination does the work. Hemingway himself described a similar idea, sometimes called the "iceberg theory": a writer who knows his subject well can omit much of it, and the reader will still sense what lies beneath the surface. Many writing teachers express the same idea with the phrase "show, don't tell". Rather than stating that a character is lonely, a writer might describe him setting the table for two out of habit, then slowly putting one plate away. Rather than declaring that a city is poor, she might describe children playing football with a ball made of plastic bags. Of course, the rule can be overused. Sometimes the clearest, most efficient choice is simply to tell. But the six-word story reminds us of something worth remembering in any kind of writing, from novels to emails: readers are not passive recipients of information. Given the right details, they will build the world themselves.

Before watching a film, millions of people check a score — the percentage of positive reviews on an aggregator site, or the star rating on a streaming platform. These numbers are useful, but they can be misleading. First, a high percentage doesn't necessarily mean a film is outstanding; it means most critics found it at least acceptable. A film that nobody loves but nobody hates can score higher than a bold, divisive masterpiece. Second, audience ratings can be manipulated. There have been well-documented cases of "review bombing", in which groups of users deliberately flood a film with negative ratings, sometimes before it has even been released. And third, critics and audiences often disagree. Some films are critically acclaimed but commercially unsuccessful; others are box-office hits that critics dismiss. My advice? Don't rely on a single number. Read two or three reviews from critics whose taste you know — and remember that disagreement is part of the pleasure of art.

In an age of star ratings and thumbs-up icons, the traditional film critic can seem like an endangered species. Many newspapers have reduced their arts coverage, and audiences increasingly rely on algorithms and influencers to decide what to watch. Some argue that critics have become irrelevant — or worse, that they are snobbish gatekeepers out of touch with what ordinary people enjoy. It is worth defending them, however, and especially their least popular product: the negative review. A thoughtful bad review is not simply an expression of dislike. At its best, it is an explanation — of why a story feels unconvincing, why a performance seems mechanical, why a film that cost hundreds of millions to make leaves no lasting impression. In explaining their disappointment, critics help readers understand what makes art work, and sharpen their own judgement in the process. Negative reviews also perform a useful function in an industry dominated by marketing. Studios spend enormous sums persuading audiences that every release is unmissable. Independent criticism offers a counterweight to that pressure, reminding us that our time and money are limited. Of course, criticism can be unfair, careless or simply cruel. A review that ridicules without explaining contributes little. And critics are not infallible: history is full of works that were dismissed on release and later recognized as masterpieces. But the solution to bad criticism is better criticism, not none at all. In the end, a culture in which everything is "amazing" is a culture in which nothing is. The willingness to say "this doesn't work, and here's why" may be one of the most valuable things a critic can offer.

Laughter itself appears to be universal. Babies laugh long before they can speak, and researchers have observed play vocalizations resembling laughter in apes and other animals. But what people find funny varies enormously. British humour, for instance, is famous for understatement and irony. Saying "It's a bit damp" during a flood is, for many Britons, both funny and polite. Many Americans, by contrast, are often described as preferring a more direct, energetic style. In Brazil, humour is frequently warm and teasing, and it's often used to cope with difficult situations — there's a long tradition of making jokes about politics, inflation and everyday frustrations. Interestingly, what travels best across cultures tends to be physical comedy. Charlie Chaplin and Mr. Bean are loved almost everywhere, partly because they don't depend on words. Puns and wordplay, on the other hand, are notoriously difficult to translate. So, if you want to be funny in another language, my advice is: start with self-deprecation and situations people recognize, and save the puns for later.

Why do we laugh? For a phenomenon so familiar, humour has proved surprisingly difficult to explain. Philosophers have offered several theories over the centuries. The oldest, associated with Plato and Thomas Hobbes, is the "superiority theory": we laugh at the misfortunes or foolishness of others because it makes us feel superior. This arguably explains slapstick and some teasing, but it hardly accounts for a clever pun. A second explanation, the "relief theory", linked to Sigmund Freud among others, suggests that laughter releases nervous energy or suppressed feelings — which may explain why people sometimes laugh at funerals or after a frightening experience. The most widely discussed today, however, is the "incongruity theory": we laugh when something violates our expectations in a way that makes sense on second thought. A punchline works because it forces us to reinterpret what came before. More recently, the researchers Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren proposed what they call the "benign violation theory". According to this idea, something is funny when it is simultaneously wrong in some way — a violation of how things should be — and yet harmless, or benign. Tickling is a good illustration: a mild physical "attack" that is clearly not dangerous. The theory also helps explain why a joke can fail in two opposite ways. If it is too safe, it is boring; if the violation feels too real or too painful, it is offensive. Needless to say, no theory captures everything. Humour depends heavily on context, culture and timing, and attempts to analyse a joke tend, ironically, to kill it. As the American writer E. B. White reportedly put it, analysing humour is like dissecting a frog: few people are interested, and the frog dies.

In October 2018, at an auction at Sotheby's in London, a framed copy of Banksy's Girl with Balloon was sold for just over one million pounds. What happened next stunned the room. Moments after the hammer came down, an alarm sounded and the canvas began to slide through a shredder hidden inside the frame. Halfway through, the shredder stopped. Banksy later posted a video suggesting that he had built the device years earlier, in case the work was ever put up for auction. Many people assumed the stunt would destroy the painting's value. What it actually did was the opposite. The half-shredded work was renamed Love is in the Bin, and in 2021 it was sold again — this time for more than eighteen million pounds. The reason it became so valuable is that the shredding itself became part of the artwork, and, arguably, part of art history. It's not that the art market missed the joke; it's that the market turned the joke into a product.

In 2019, at the Art Basel fair in Miami, the Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan exhibited a work called Comedian: a real banana, attached to a wall with grey duct tape. Editions of the work were reportedly sold for around 120,000 dollars each. Then, to the delight of photographers, a performance artist peeled the banana off the wall and ate it. The gallery was unconcerned. What the buyers had purchased, it explained, was not the fruit itself but a certificate of authenticity and instructions for replacing it. The episode provoked a familiar mixture of laughter and outrage. For many people, it confirmed their suspicion that contemporary art is a joke played on the rich. Yet the story raises a serious question: where does the value of art actually lie? It is not that the materials of most great art are especially precious; paint, canvas and stone are relatively cheap. What we pay for, arguably, is something less tangible: an idea, a reputation, a story, a moment in history. Vincent van Gogh is often said to have sold only one painting in his lifetime — an oversimplification, but one that captures how little his work was valued while he lived. Today, his paintings rank among the most expensive ever sold. Nothing about the canvases changed. What changed was how people saw them. None of this means that every expensive work is a masterpiece, or that every unknown artist is a misunderstood genius. Markets can be driven by fashion, speculation and the desire for status. But perhaps the banana on the wall was doing exactly what art has always done: making us look again at something ordinary and ask what it means. The thing is, whether that is worth 120,000 dollars is a question no theory can answer for us.

For decades, scientists have warned that the Amazon rainforest may be approaching a critical threshold. The concept is relatively simple. The forest generates a large share of its own rainfall: trees release moisture into the air, which forms clouds that carry rain further inland. As deforestation and climate change reduce the number of trees and increase temperatures, this cycle weakens. Beyond a certain point — a "tipping point" — parts of the forest could be unable to sustain themselves and might gradually turn into a drier, savannah-like ecosystem. Estimates of where exactly that point lies vary. In widely cited work, the Brazilian climate scientist Carlos Nobre and the American biologist Thomas Lovejoy suggested that it might be reached if deforestation exceeded around 20 to 25 percent of the original forest. Some studies indicate that parts of the eastern Amazon are already showing signs of stress, with longer dry seasons and, in certain areas, the forest releasing more carbon than it absorbs. Not all researchers agree on how close the tipping point is, and the forest is likely to respond differently from region to region. What is broadly accepted, however, is that the consequences of large-scale dieback would extend far beyond the Amazon itself. Rainfall in other parts of South America, including Brazil's agricultural heartland, depends partly on moisture from the forest. There are reasons for cautious hope. Deforestation rates have fallen significantly in some recent years, demonstrating that policy and enforcement can make a difference. Restoration projects are also under way. But if the Amazon is to remain a rainforest, many scientists argue, the next two decades are likely to be decisive.

Brazil has been shaped by migration — much of it forced. Over three centuries, an estimated four to five million enslaved Africans were brought to Brazil, more than to any other country in the Americas. Their descendants account for a large part of today's population, and African influences run through Brazilian culture, from music and religion to food and language. From the late nineteenth century, a new wave of immigration began, much of it brought about by government policies to attract European labour after the abolition of slavery in 1888. Italians, Portuguese, Spaniards and Germans arrived in large numbers, followed by Japanese immigrants from 1908 — today, Brazil is home to the largest population of Japanese descent outside Japan. Lebanese and Syrian communities also set down deep roots. In recent decades, the picture has changed again: Brazil has received people from Haiti, Venezuela, Bolivia and African countries, while hundreds of thousands of Brazilians have themselves emigrated, to places such as the United States, Portugal and Japan.

Few issues provoke as much political debate as migration, and few are as widely misunderstood. Public opinion surveys in many countries suggest that people tend to overestimate the number of immigrants living among them, sometimes considerably. Much of the anxiety surrounding migration stems from economic fears: that newcomers will take jobs, push down wages or place an unbearable burden on public services. What does the evidence say? On the question of jobs, most economic research has failed to bear out the most pessimistic predictions. Migrants often take up work that local workers are unwilling or unavailable to do, or set up businesses that create new employment. Their effect on average wages is generally found to be small, although some studies point to modest negative effects for specific groups of low-skilled workers, particularly in the short term. Migrants also tend to be of working age, which means that, in ageing societies, they can help to pay for pensions and healthcare. At the same time, it would be naive to rule out real challenges. Rapid arrivals can put pressure on housing, schools and health services in particular areas, especially when governments fail to plan or invest accordingly. Integration does not happen automatically: newcomers frequently come up against language barriers, unrecognized qualifications and discrimination, all of which can prevent them from contributing fully. Emigration, meanwhile, has its own consequences for countries of origin. The "brain drain" of doctors, engineers and other professionals can weaken health and education systems, although remittances sent home by migrants account for a substantial share of income in many developing economies. Ultimately, the evidence suggests that migration is neither the catastrophe some fear nor the simple solution others claim. Its effects depend largely on how societies choose to face up to it.

In 2018, a team of researchers at MIT published a study in the journal Science that analysed around 126,000 stories shared on Twitter between 2006 and 2017. Each story had been checked by independent fact-checking organizations. The findings were striking. False stories were found to spread significantly further, faster and more widely than true ones. According to the study, false news was about 70 percent more likely to be retweeted than the truth. Why? The researchers suggested that false stories tend to be more novel and surprising, and that they provoke stronger emotional reactions, such as disgust and fear. Interestingly, the study concluded that it was humans, not automated bots, who were primarily responsible for the difference. Bots were found to spread true and false stories at similar rates. The implication is uncomfortable. If we want to fight misinformation, it is not enough to blame algorithms or foreign agents. We also have to look at our own behaviour — and pause before we click "share".

In 2018, a video appeared online in which former US president Barack Obama seemed to insult his successor. The video was not real. It had been created by the media company BuzzFeed, in collaboration with the filmmaker Jordan Peele, who voiced the words, to warn the public about a new kind of technology: deepfakes. Since then, the tools needed to produce convincing fake video and audio have become dramatically cheaper and easier to use. What once required a professional studio can now reportedly be done in minutes with a laptop or even a phone. The consequences are already visible. Fake audio recordings of politicians have allegedly been circulated shortly before elections in several countries, when there is little time to debunk them. Criminals are reported to have used cloned voices of company executives to persuade employees to transfer money. Ordinary people, too, have been targeted with fabricated images. Perhaps the most worrying effect, however, is not that people will believe fake content but that they will stop believing real content. Researchers have called this the "liar's dividend": when anything could be fake, those caught on camera doing something wrong can simply claim that the evidence has been fabricated. Truth itself becomes a matter of opinion. There are responses. Technology companies are said to be developing tools to detect manipulated media and to label AI-generated content, and several governments have introduced or proposed regulations. Journalists and fact-checkers are increasingly trained in verification techniques. But most experts concede that technology alone cannot solve the problem. In the end, the best defence may be an old-fashioned one: a healthy scepticism, combined with trust in reliable, accountable sources.

At C1 level, the difference between a good essay and an excellent one is often not the ideas but the organization. We assess writing in four areas: content, communicative achievement, organization and language. Under organization, we're looking for a text that is well structured and cohesive, using a variety of devices — not just linking words. Many candidates think that the more "furthermore" and "moreover" they use, the higher their score will be. In fact, overusing linking words can make a text feel mechanical. What really impresses examiners is when ideas flow naturally: when a sentence refers back to the previous one using "this problem" or "such an approach", and when paragraphs are connected by a clear line of argument. The other common mistake is forgetting part of the task. In the essay, you must clearly state which option you consider more important, and give reasons. If you don't, your content score will suffer, however good your English is.

Over half of the world's population now lives in cities, and this proportion is expected to keep rising. As a result, the question of how to make urban life healthier and more sustainable has become increasingly urgent. Of the various measures available to governments, investment in public transport and the provision of affordable housing are two of the most frequently discussed.. . An efficient public transport system can transform daily life. When buses and trains are frequent, safe and affordable, fewer people depend on cars, which in turn reduces congestion, air pollution and carbon emissions. Such a network also widens access to jobs and education, particularly for those living on the outskirts. However, this kind of infrastructure is costly and can take years to build, and its benefits depend heavily on good planning and maintenance.. . Affordable housing, by contrast, addresses a more fundamental need. In many cities, soaring rents have pushed low-income families into informal settlements or distant suburbs, where they face long commutes and limited services. Providing decent homes closer to city centres would not only improve living conditions but also reduce the very travel demands that transport investment seeks to meet. Admittedly, such programmes can be poorly managed and may concentrate poverty if they are badly designed.. . On balance, although both measures are valuable, I believe the latter should be the priority. Without a secure, affordable place to live, people cannot fully benefit from any other improvement a city has to offer. Moreover, well-located housing reduces the need for long journeys in the first place, making it, in the long term, the more far-reaching solution.

In 1981, Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project published Getting to Yes, a book that became one of the most influential guides to negotiation ever written. Their central idea was to move away from what they called "positional bargaining", where each side digs in and defends a fixed position, towards "principled negotiation". This rests on a few key principles. First, separate the people from the problem: you can be tough on the issue while remaining respectful to the person. Second, focus on interests, not positions. Two people might both demand the same orange — but if one wants the juice and the other wants the peel for a cake, there's a solution that satisfies both. Third, invent options for mutual gain before deciding. And fourth, insist on objective criteria, such as market prices or expert opinion, rather than a contest of wills. Diplomatic language is essential here. It allows you to challenge ideas without attacking people — which is often what makes agreement possible.

Every culture has its own rules about how directly people should express disagreement, and misunderstandings between cultures can be costly. In her influential book The Culture Map, Erin Meyer, a professor at the business school INSEAD, describes a scale ranging from cultures where negative feedback is delivered directly to those where it is delivered indirectly. In the Netherlands, Israel and Germany, she argues, people tend to give criticism frankly, often using "upgraders" such as "absolutely" or "totally": "This is totally inappropriate." In the United Kingdom, Japan and much of Southeast Asia, by contrast, criticism is typically softened with "downgraders": "This might be slightly inappropriate." The problem arises when the two styles meet. A Dutch manager who tells a British colleague that his presentation was "a bit weak" may think she is being helpful; the British colleague may hear something far more devastating, because in his culture "a bit weak" is how one might describe a disaster. Conversely, a British manager who describes a project as "not quite what we were hoping for" may be shocked to discover that a Dutch employee interpreted this as minor feedback. Brazil occupies an interesting position. Brazilians are often described as expressive and warm, and comfortable showing emotion. Yet when it comes to negative feedback, especially towards superiors or in public, many Brazilians tend to soften their message considerably — sometimes so much that the criticism is missed entirely. The lesson is not that one style is superior. It is that effective communicators learn to recognize the code being used and, when necessary, check their understanding. A simple question — "Just to make sure I understand, are you saying that we need to redo this?" — can prevent a great deal of confusion.

Most teams evaluate risks by asking, "What could go wrong?" The problem is that, once a team is excited about a project, few people want to be seen as negative. The psychologist Gary Klein proposed a clever alternative called the "pre-mortem". Before making a final decision, the team imagines that it's a year later and the project has failed completely. Then each person writes down, independently, the reasons why it failed. Research on what's called "prospective hindsight" suggests that imagining that an event has already happened can make it easier to identify its causes. So instead of "Were we to fail, what might the reasons be?", you say, "We failed. Why?" People suddenly feel free to mention concerns they'd otherwise keep to themselves. Had more organizations used this technique, many expensive disasters might have been avoided. And it costs nothing but an hour of honest conversation.

In her book Thinking in Bets, the former professional poker player Annie Duke argues that most of us make a fundamental mistake when judging our decisions: we evaluate them by their outcomes. Poker players call this "resulting". If a decision turns out well, we assume it was a good one; if it turns out badly, we conclude it was a mistake. But, as Duke points out, the quality of a decision and the quality of its outcome are not the same thing. Imagine you drive home after drinking too much and arrive safely. Was it a good decision? Clearly not. Had you crashed, nobody would have questioned that conclusion; the fact that you were lucky does not change it. Conversely, a well-reasoned business decision might fail for reasons nobody could have foreseen. Were we to judge every choice purely by what happened afterwards, we would learn the wrong lessons from both. The alternative, Duke suggests, is to think of decisions as bets on an uncertain future. Before deciding, ask: what are the possible outcomes, how likely is each, and what would each cost or gain me? Assuming you have made a reasonable estimate with the information available, you have made a good decision — whatever happens next. This way of thinking has practical benefits. It encourages people to seek out information that might prove them wrong, to admit uncertainty ("I'm about 70 percent sure") and to review their decisions more honestly. Should a plan fail, the question becomes not "Who is to blame?" but "Was this bad luck, bad information or bad judgement?" Given that almost every important decision in life involves uncertainty, that may be one of the most useful questions we can learn to ask.

Linguists use the term "register" to describe the way language varies according to its context: who is speaking to whom, about what, and through which medium. We all switch registers constantly, usually without thinking. The same person might say "Could you possibly pass the salt?" at a formal dinner, "Pass the salt, please" at home and simply "Salt?" to a close friend. For language learners, however, register can be a hidden trap. Textbooks often teach a fairly neutral style, while films and social media expose learners to very informal speech. The result can be an awkward mixture: an email to a university professor that begins "Hey!" or a casual chat sprinkled with expressions like "furthermore" and "I hereby". Neither is grammatically wrong, but both send an unintended social message. English has a particular feature that makes register especially noticeable: its double vocabulary. After the Norman Conquest of 1066, French became the language of the ruling class in England for centuries, while English continued to be spoken by ordinary people. As a result, English today often has two words for the same idea — a shorter, everyday word of Germanic origin and a longer, more formal one from French or Latin: help and assist, buy and purchase, ask and enquire, begin and commence. A famous illustration involves animals and food. The farm animals kept by English-speaking peasants have Germanic names — cow, pig, sheep — while the meat served at aristocratic tables took French-derived names: beef, pork, mutton. Mastering register, then, is not about learning to be formal. It is about choosing the right words for the right situation. A C1 speaker is not someone who always sounds sophisticated, but someone who knows when not to.

That's a fascinating question. I can see why people might think so — the tools have become remarkably accurate. That said, I'd argue that a language isn't just a code to be translated. What you lose with an app is the nuance: humour, irony, the things people leave unsaid.

Reaching C1 is a remarkable achievement. According to the CEFR, a C1 user can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, recognize implicit meaning, express themselves fluently and spontaneously, and use language flexibly for social, academic and professional purposes. But what comes next? Progress beyond this level tends to be slower and less visible, which can be frustrating. You no longer learn new grammar every week; instead, you refine. My advice is threefold. First, read widely — novels, long-form journalism, academic articles — because this is where your vocabulary will grow most. Second, specialize: develop the English of your profession or passion in depth. And third, use English to create, not just to consume: write, present, debate, teach. Interestingly, many highly proficient speakers say the moment they felt truly fluent wasn't when they passed an exam. It was when they laughed at a joke without having to think — or when they realized they'd been dreaming in English.

Almost every advanced learner eventually encounters what teachers call the "intermediate plateau" — and its more subtle cousin, the advanced plateau. In the early stages of learning a language, progress is fast and obvious: every week brings new words, new structures and new abilities. At higher levels, however, the gains become smaller and harder to notice. Learners who could once measure their improvement in leaps now find it difficult to see any improvement at all. Part of the explanation is that the remaining gaps are less visible. A B1 learner knows when she does not understand a sentence. A C1 learner usually understands, but may not notice that a native speaker would have chosen a different collocation, a more precise verb or a subtler level of politeness. Such gaps rarely cause communication to break down, which means there is little pressure to fix them. Research on expertise offers some useful insights. The psychologist Anders Ericsson, whose work on expert performance became widely known, argued that improvement at advanced levels depends less on the amount of practice than on its quality. What he called "deliberate practice" involves working on specific weaknesses, at the edge of one's ability, with immediate feedback. For language learners, this might mean recording yourself and comparing your speech with a model, rewriting a paragraph three times in different registers, or noting down every unfamiliar collocation you meet in a week. Equally important is motivation. At C1, the external rewards — passing an exam, getting a job — have often already been achieved. Learners who continue to improve tend to be those who have found intrinsic reasons: a love of literature, an international friendship, a professional passion. In the end, the plateau is not a wall but a change of terrain. The climb continues; it simply requires a different kind of walking.

In a classic experiment published in 1974, the psychologists Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed participants films of car accidents and then asked them how fast the cars were going. The only difference between the groups was a single verb. Some were asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed into" each other; others heard "collided", "bumped", "hit" or "contacted". Those who heard "smashed" gave the highest speed estimates. A week later, they were also more likely to report having seen broken glass — even though there was none in the film. One word changed not just how people judged the event, but what they remembered. Journalists, lawyers and politicians understand this intuitively. Is a sudden rise in prices a "spike" or a "correction"? Are people who cross a border "migrants", "refugees" or "illegals"? Each choice is a small argument in disguise. And at the highest level of language, noticing those choices — and making them consciously — is perhaps the most important skill of all.

Every writing teacher has encountered it: the essay in which every second word appears to have been lifted from a thesaurus. "The protagonist perambulated pensively through the verdant arboretum", writes the student, when what he means is that the main character walked through the park, thinking. The impulse is understandable. Learners — and, for that matter, many native speakers — are often taught that variety is a virtue and that repetition is a sin. A thesaurus seems to offer an endless supply of alternatives. The difficulty is that a thesaurus lists words that are similar, not words that are interchangeable. "Slender", "skinny", "gaunt" and "emaciated" all denote thinness, but they evoke four very different people. "Notorious" and "famous" both describe someone widely known, yet only one would be welcome on a reference letter. Even apparently neutral synonyms differ in collocation and register: one "commences" a legal procedure but rarely "commences" a holiday. Linguists sometimes claim that there are no true synonyms in any language — that if two words were genuinely identical in every context, one of them would eventually fall out of use or acquire a distinct meaning. Whether or not this is strictly true, it captures something important. Words carry histories, associations and social signals that no list can fully record. The solution is not to abandon the thesaurus but to treat it as a starting point rather than an answer. Before adopting an unfamiliar word, a careful writer checks how it is actually used: in which contexts, with which neighbours, in what tone. Precision, not variety, is the hallmark of good writing — and, at the highest levels of proficiency, of good speaking too. As the novelist Elmore Leonard memorably advised: if it sounds like writing, rewrite it.

In the 1960s and 1970s, the British philosopher Paul Grice proposed that conversation is guided by what he called the Cooperative Principle. We assume that the people we talk to are trying to communicate efficiently, and he described several "maxims" they generally follow: say as much as is needed but no more; say what you believe to be true; be relevant; and be clear. The fascinating part is what happens when someone appears to break a maxim. Suppose I ask a friend, "How was the restaurant?" and she replies, "Well, the parking was easy." She's apparently being irrelevant. But because I assume she's cooperating, I infer something she hasn't said: the food was by no means good. Grice called this kind of meaning an "implicature". It's how irony works, how politeness works, and how a great deal of everyday communication works. And it's often where advanced learners struggle — not with the words, but with what lies between them.

English, and British English in particular, has a reputation for understatement, and few devices capture this more neatly than litotes: the practice of asserting something by denying its opposite. To describe a brilliant performance as "not bad", a catastrophic error as "not ideal" or a significant achievement as "no mean feat" is to communicate, paradoxically, by appearing to say less than one means. The device is far from new. It appears in Old English poetry, where a hero might be said to be "not unfamiliar" with battle, and it was a favourite of classical rhetoricians, who valued it as a way of sounding modest while making a strong point. Why should speakers choose such an indirect route? Part of the answer lies in social risk. Unrestrained praise can sound insincere; unrestrained criticism can sound aggressive. Litotes offers a way of expressing judgement while leaving room for retreat. A manager who calls a report "not without its problems" can, if challenged, insist that she meant only minor issues — even if both parties know she meant something rather more serious. There is also an aesthetic dimension. Understatement invites the listener to participate, to reconstruct the full meaning from the restrained version. When it works, it creates a sense of shared understanding, almost of complicity. Yet the same quality makes litotes treacherous for anyone unfamiliar with the code. A visitor who takes "not bad" at face value may underestimate genuine enthusiasm, while one who takes "it's not the worst idea I've heard" as encouragement may be in for a disappointment. At the highest levels of proficiency, then, understanding English is by no means simply a matter of knowing words. It is a matter of knowing how much — and how little — they are being asked to carry.

Why do English speakers say "salt and pepper" but never "pepper and salt"? Or "rock and roll", "black and white", "ladies and gentlemen"? Linguists have identified several tendencies — not strict rules, but strong patterns. First, the shorter word tends to come first: "salt and pepper", "bread and butter". Second, when vowels differ, words with higher, front vowels — like the "i" in "zig" — tend to precede lower, back vowels, like the "a" in "zag". That's why it's "zig-zag", "tick-tock", "flip-flop" and never the other way round. Third, cultural or logical priority often matters: "cause and effect", "before and after", "husband and wife" — though the last example also shows how these orders can reflect social hierarchies of the past. Interestingly, Portuguese often shows similar patterns. But when the orders differ between languages, learners tend to transfer their own — which is why, at C2, these small, fixed pairs are worth learning as single units.

Few writers handle fixed expressions with as much mischief as the authors of newspaper headlines. Limited to a handful of words and competing for the reader's attention, headline writers — sub-editors, in British newsrooms — have long relied on a simple trick: take a familiar phrase and twist it. A story about a theft from a cheese factory becomes "Grate Expectations"; an article on the decline of hand-written letters is headed "Signed, Sealed, Deleted"; a report on rising house prices in a seaside town appears as "Home and Dry? Not Any More". The technique depends entirely on recognition. The reader must instantly recall the original — Dickens's Great Expectations, the song "Signed, Sealed, Delivered", the idiom "home and dry" — and register the change. The pleasure lies in the gap between the expected and the actual, and in the small flash of understanding that bridges it. Advertising uses the same mechanism, as do comedians, politicians and, increasingly, social media users. For language learners, this presents a particular challenge. It is perfectly possible to understand every word of a headline and still miss its point entirely. A learner unfamiliar with "Every cloud has a silver lining" will find nothing remarkable in a technology column titled "Every Cloud Has a Cyber Lining"; the native reader, by contrast, sees a joke, an argument and a cultural reference compressed into six words. This is why fixed expressions matter far more at the highest levels than their apparent triviality might suggest. They are part and parcel of a shared cultural memory — the background against which a great deal of creative language is written. To read like an insider, one must first know what the insiders know by heart. Only then can one appreciate, and eventually produce, the twist.

What separates great travel writing from a guidebook? Generally speaking, it's the shift from information to experience. A guidebook tells you the museum opens at nine. A travel writer puts you on the steps outside at ten to nine, the street still wet from the night's rain, a stray dog asleep in a patch of sunlight. Notice the grammar there — those little phrases with their own subjects, "the street still wet", "a dog asleep". They let a writer add layers of detail without stopping the flow of the sentence. Writers like Jan Morris, Bruce Chatwin and Paul Theroux used them constantly. The other ingredient is honesty. The best travel writers aren't afraid to describe disappointment, boredom or their own prejudices — and, all things considered, that's what makes us trust them when they describe wonder.

I arrived in Ouro Preto after midnight, the bus from Belo Horizonte having been delayed by fog on the mountain road, and I remember almost nothing of that first night except the cold and the sound of rain on a tiled roof. It was the morning that stayed with me. I woke before six, the room still dark, and, unable to sleep, went out to walk. The town, built on hills so steep that some streets seem to defy gravity, was entirely silent. Mist lay in the valleys between the churches, their towers rising out of it like the masts of ships at anchor. The cobblestones, polished by three centuries of feet and that night's rain, shone under the last of the streetlamps. Somewhere below, a dog barked once, then thought better of it. I climbed towards the Church of São Francisco de Assis, my breath visible in the air, my legs protesting at every step. With the light growing stronger, details began to emerge: the soapstone carvings above the doorway, the blue and white of colonial façades, a woman in a doorway sweeping her front step, her radio murmuring a morning programme. She nodded to me without a word, as if strangers at dawn were part and parcel of her day. History in Ouro Preto is not a subject but an atmosphere. Gold made the town rich in the eighteenth century, its wealth flowing to Lisbon and beyond, and the beauty that remains was built, in large part, by enslaved labour — a fact no honest visitor should forget. Yet that morning, the streets empty and the mist slowly lifting, it felt less like a museum than a place still dreaming. By eight, the first tour buses had arrived. The spell broken, I went in search of coffee. All things considered, I have rarely spent two hours better.

You may have heard of Aristotle's three modes of persuasion: ethos, the character and credibility of the speaker; pathos, the emotions of the audience; and logos, the logic of the argument. Less well known, but no less important, is a fourth concept the Greeks discussed: kairos, the opportune moment. Such is the importance of timing that the same words can inspire a nation on one day and fall completely flat on another. Think of a leader addressing the country after a disaster. Rarely is an audience more ready to listen, and rarely does a speaker have more power — or more responsibility. Gone, of course, are the days when a speech reached people only once, in a hall or on the radio. Today, every phrase can be clipped, replayed and reinterpreted in a different context, months or years later. Kairos has become far more complicated. A sentence that was perfectly judged at the time may sound tone-deaf when it resurfaces. Nowhere is this more evident than on social media.

Gone are the days when political arguments unfolded over hours. In nineteenth-century America, the famous debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas could last three hours, with each candidate speaking for an hour or more while crowds stood and listened. Such was the appetite for political oratory that newspapers printed the speeches in full, and readers studied them line by line. The contrast with today could hardly be sharper. Studies of American television news have documented a dramatic shrinking of the "soundbite" — the length of time a candidate is shown speaking without interruption. According to research frequently cited by media scholars, the average soundbite on the evening news fell from more than forty seconds in the late 1960s to under ten seconds by the end of the 1980s. Social media has accelerated the trend still further. Today, a political career can be made or broken by a phrase short enough to fit on a placard. What has been lost? Critics argue that complexity is the first casualty. Few serious problems — climate change, healthcare, inequality — can be explained in a single sentence, and politicians who attempt to do so are forced to oversimplify. Equally worrying is the effect on public trust. When every statement is designed to be clipped and shared, politicians speak less to persuade than to avoid giving their opponents ammunition. Yet it would be wrong to romanticize the past. Long speeches were by no means guaranteed to be wise, and many nineteenth-century orators were skilled demagogues. Nor is brevity always a vice: some of the most powerful phrases in political history are also among the shortest. Perhaps the real question is not how long political speech should be, but whether audiences still have the patience — and the platforms — to hear arguments that cannot be reduced to a slogan.

In 1946, George Orwell published an essay called "Politics and the English Language". His argument was that political language is often designed to make the indefensible sound reasonable. He gave examples from his own time: villages bombed and inhabitants driven out were described as "pacification". Rather than describe brutal events directly, officials reached for abstract, Latinate words that created a kind of fog. Orwell also attacked lazy writing more generally — dying metaphors, pretentious vocabulary, unnecessary passives — because he believed that sloppy language makes sloppy thinking easier. He ended with six rules, the most famous of which is probably: "Never use a long word where a short one will do." He was also honest enough to add a final rule allowing writers to break any of the others rather than say anything outright barbarous. Almost eighty years later, the essay is still widely read, and its central warning still applies. When language stops describing reality and starts concealing it, democracy has a problem.
