Few genres of public communication have been studied as closely, or mocked as mercilessly, as the corporate apology. When a company is caught polluting a river, mistreating customers or leaking personal data, its statement tends to follow a predictable pattern — one that linguists and public relations experts have learned to dissect. It typically begins with an expression of regret, rather than an apology: "We regret any inconvenience this may have caused." The verb "regret" is significant. One can regret a storm; regret does not imply responsibility. The phrase "any inconvenience" minimizes the harm, while "may have caused" leaves open the possibility that nothing was caused at all. Next comes the passive voice. "Mistakes were made" and "data was accessed" describe events without naming anyone who performed them. The agent — the company, its executives, a specific decision — quietly vanishes from the sentence. Then there is the conditional apology: "We apologize to anyone who was affected" or "We're sorry if customers felt let down." By placing the problem in the reactions of others, the statement implies that the fault lies, at least partly, in their sensitivity. Finally, the statement moves swiftly to the future: "We are committed to the highest standards and are reviewing our processes." The past, with all its awkward details, is left behind. Research on apologies suggests that the most effective ones do almost exactly the opposite. They acknowledge responsibility clearly, name the specific harm, express genuine remorse, explain what went wrong and offer concrete repair. They are short, specific and active. "We broke your trust. Here is what we did, here is why it happened, and here is what we will do to put it right." Such apologies are rare, not because they are hard to write, but because they are hard to say. They require something the language of spin is designed to avoid: accepting the blame.

Almost everyone clicks "I agree" without reading. In one well-known experiment, published in 2016, researchers Jonathan Obar and Anne Oeldorf-Hirsch created a fictitious social network and asked students to sign up. Buried in the terms of service was a clause whereby users agreed to give up their first-born child as payment. The overwhelming majority of participants agreed — most of them, apparently, without noticing. The study was, admittedly, an exaggeration, albeit a revealing one. Real terms of service rarely demand children, but they frequently contain provisions whereby users waive important rights: allowing companies to share data with third parties, to change the terms at any time, or to resolve disputes through private arbitration rather than in court. Several jurisdictions, including the European Union, have introduced rules requiring that key information be presented clearly, thereby giving consumers a better chance of understanding what they're signing. Notwithstanding these efforts, the basic problem remains: terms are long, readers are busy, and the default is to trust.

Few styles of writing are as widely disliked as "legalese": the dense, archaic and seemingly impenetrable language of contracts, statutes and terms of service. Critics have long argued that it serves mainly to exclude ordinary readers, thereby protecting the interests of lawyers and the powerful. Movements for "plain language" in law have won significant victories, and in many countries, government documents and consumer contracts must now be written in a way that the average reader can understand. Yet legal language is not merely the product of tradition or self-interest. Many of its peculiarities exist for a reason. Words such as "notwithstanding", "hereinafter" and "whereby" allow drafters to establish precise relationships between different parts of a document — which clause overrides which, how a term is defined, by what mechanism an obligation arises. Ordinary words, by contrast, tend to be vague, and vagueness in a contract can lead to years of costly litigation. Repetition, too, has a purpose: a lawyer who writes "the Buyer" fifty times rather than switching to "they" or "the customer" ensures that no court can later argue that the parties meant different people. Some features, admittedly, are harder to defend. Doublets and triplets such as "null and void", "cease and desist" and "give, devise and bequeath" are largely historical relics, dating from a time when English law drew on English, French and Latin and drafters used all three to be safe. Long sentences with multiple embedded clauses serve the convenience of the writer far more than the comprehension of the reader. The challenge, then, is not to abolish legal language but to distinguish precision from obscurity. A good contract should be as exact as necessary — albeit no more complicated than it needs to be. Insofar as plain language can achieve that, it is not the enemy of the law but its ally.

On 19 November 1863, at the dedication of a military cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, Abraham Lincoln spoke for around two minutes. The main speaker that day, the celebrated orator Edward Everett, had spoken for about two hours. It is Lincoln's speech that is remembered. Why? Partly because of its brevity — fewer than three hundred words — and partly because of its extraordinary craftsmanship. Lincoln uses antithesis repeatedly: the world "will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here." He uses a tricolon of verbs: "we can not dedicate — we can not consecrate — we can not hallow — this ground." And he ends with perhaps the most famous example of epistrophe in American history, describing a government "of the people, by the people, for the people". Notice, too, the irony of that first antithesis: Lincoln claimed the world would not remember his words. Rarely has a prediction been so completely wrong.

For much of Western history, rhetoric — the art of persuasive speech — stood at the centre of education. Roman schoolboys practised declamation; medieval universities taught it as one of the three foundational arts, alongside grammar and logic; and well into the nineteenth century, educated people were expected to recognize, and to use, figures such as anaphora and chiasmus. In the twentieth century, however, rhetoric acquired a bad name. After decades of wartime propaganda and, later, the polished manipulations of advertising, the word came to suggest empty or deceptive speech: "mere rhetoric". Many schools quietly dropped it from the curriculum. This is unfortunate, for two reasons. First, the techniques of rhetoric have not disappeared; they have simply become less visible. Every political speech, advertising campaign and viral post draws on the same toolkit that Cicero and Quintilian described two thousand years ago. Citizens who cannot recognize these techniques are, in a sense, defenceless against them. To identify a false antithesis — "either you are with us or you are against us" — is already to begin to resist it. Second, rhetoric is not only a weapon of the powerful. It has also been the instrument of those seeking to challenge power. Abolitionists, suffragists and civil rights leaders were, almost without exception, masters of persuasive language; their speeches combined moral clarity with carefully crafted rhythm, repetition and contrast. To dismiss rhetoric as manipulation is, in effect, to give up one of the most effective tools of democratic change. Perhaps the solution is to return rhetoric to its original place: not as a set of tricks but as a discipline of both speaking and listening. A society that teaches its citizens to recognize persuasion, to analyse it and to use it responsibly is far better equipped to govern itself than one that merely hopes its leaders will speak honestly.

In the 1960s, an analyst at the CIA, Sherman Kent, noticed a worrying problem. Intelligence reports used words like "probable", "likely" and "a serious possibility", but when he asked colleagues what probability these words represented, their answers varied enormously. For some, "a serious possibility" meant a 20 percent chance; for others, 80. Later surveys of the general public have found the same pattern. The word "likely" might mean 60 percent to one person and 90 to another. This matters. A doctor who says a treatment will "probably" work, or a climate report that describes an outcome as "very likely", may be understood very differently by different people. That's why some organizations — the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, for instance — attach specific numerical ranges to their words: "very likely", in their reports, means 90 to 100 percent. The lesson for all of us? When it really matters, it's worth adding a number.

In the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, scientists faced a communication challenge of unprecedented scale. They were being asked, daily and in front of enormous audiences, to answer questions that could not yet be answered with confidence. How easily does the virus spread? How deadly is it? Do masks help? The honest answer to many of these questions was, at first, "We don't know — but here is what we think is likely." That answer proved remarkably difficult to communicate. Audiences, understandably, wanted certainty. Politicians often preferred clear messages. And when advice changed as evidence accumulated — as it inevitably did — many people concluded that the experts had been wrong, or worse, dishonest. Yet changing one's mind in response to new evidence is not a failure of science; it is the very essence of it. Researchers who study risk communication have drawn several lessons from the experience. First, uncertainty should be acknowledged openly and early. Studies suggest that admitting uncertainty does not necessarily damage trust; in some cases, audiences find it more credible than false confidence. Second, it helps to distinguish clearly between what is known, what is probable and what is still unknown. Third, communicators should explain in advance that advice may change, and why. If people expect revisions, they are less likely to interpret them as contradictions. None of this is easy. A message hedged with qualifications is, in all likelihood, less memorable than a confident slogan. But there is every reason to believe that, over time, honesty about uncertainty builds a deeper and more durable kind of trust — one that can survive the inevitable moments when the evidence shifts.

If you've ever struggled with an academic article, you're not alone. Corpus research led by linguists such as Douglas Biber has shown that academic writing differs from conversation in a striking way. Conversation is dominated by verbs and clauses: "We went out, and then it started raining, so we came back." Academic prose, by contrast, is dominated by nouns and noun phrases: "The sudden onset of heavy rainfall necessitated an early return." Information is packed into long, complex noun phrases, which allows writers to express a great deal very concisely — but also places heavy demands on the reader. This density isn't simply pretentiousness. It allows academics to treat processes as objects that can be discussed, compared and measured. Once "people moved to the cities" becomes "urbanization", you can ask about the rate of urbanization, the causes of urbanization, the effects of urbanization. That said, many style guides now encourage academics to balance density with clarity — and to remember that a paper nobody can read is a paper nobody will cite.

Over the past fifteen years, a growing body of research has raised uncomfortable questions about the reliability of published scientific findings. The concern, often referred to as the "replication crisis", emerged most visibly in psychology. In a large-scale collaborative project published in Science in 2015, the Open Science Collaboration attempted to reproduce one hundred studies previously published in leading psychology journals. While nearly all the original studies had reported statistically significant results, only around a third to a half of the replications, depending on the criteria used, produced comparable findings. The causes of this problem are widely debated. A number of researchers contend that the incentive structures of academic publishing bear a considerable share of the responsibility. Journals have traditionally favoured novel, positive results over replications or null findings, thereby encouraging what critics describe as "questionable research practices": analysing data in multiple ways until a significant result emerges, or reporting only the outcomes that support the original hypothesis. Others emphasize methodological factors, including small sample sizes and insufficient statistical power. Not all scholars accept the more pessimistic interpretations, however. Some have argued that the replication studies themselves suffered from methodological limitations, and that differences between original and replication findings may reflect variations in populations or procedures rather than flawed original research. These objections notwithstanding, the episode has prompted significant reforms. Pre-registration of hypotheses and analysis plans, the sharing of data and materials, and the publication of registered reports — in which journals commit to publishing a study before its results are known — have become increasingly common. Whether these measures will substantially improve the reliability of the scientific record remains, at present, an open empirical question.

For a long time, many professional historians dismissed counterfactual history as a parlour game. The British historian E. H. Carr famously mocked it, and plenty of scholars still regard it with suspicion. Yet, in a sense, all historical explanation is counterfactual. To say that an event caused another is to imply that, had the first not happened, the second would not have happened either. Suppose a historian claims that a drought caused a revolution. That claim only makes sense if we can imagine the same society without the drought — and ask whether the revolution would still have occurred. Used carefully, counterfactuals help us test explanations and resist the illusion that the past was inevitable. Used carelessly, however, they become fantasy, with each imaginary step piled on another as though we could know the consequences decades later. The trick, most historians who use them would say, is to stay close to the moment: change one thing, ask what was realistically possible, and stop before you start writing a novel.

Looking back, it is tempting to see history as a path leading inexorably towards the present. Empires rise and fall as though following a script; revolutions break out because they "had to"; technologies appear exactly when the world is ready for them. Psychologists have a name for part of this tendency: hindsight bias, the inclination, once we know an outcome, to believe that it was predictable all along. In a series of classic experiments in the 1970s, the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff found that people who were told the outcome of a historical event rated that outcome as considerably more likely than people who were not told — and frequently believed they would have predicted it themselves. Counterfactual thinking is one of the most effective antidotes to this illusion. By asking "what if?", we are forced to reconstruct the uncertainty that people at the time actually faced. Suppose an assassination attempt had failed, a ship had sailed a day earlier, or a vote had gone the other way by a handful of ballots. Would the world look the same? Very often, the honest answer is that we cannot be sure — and that uncertainty is itself a valuable insight. It reminds us that the people of the past were not characters walking towards a known ending, but individuals making difficult choices with incomplete information, much as we do. There is a moral dimension to this, too. If the past was inevitable, then nobody was truly responsible for it: things simply happened as they had to. If, on the other hand, outcomes hinged on decisions that could have been different, then those decisions — and the people who made them — can be judged. Far from being idle speculation, then, the question "what if?" may be one of the most serious questions historians, and citizens, can ask. Would that it were asked more often.

In his best-selling book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman, who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2002, popularized a useful way of describing the mind. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it recognizes a face, reads a simple sentence, or tells you instantly that two plus two is four. System 2 is slow, effortful and deliberate: it's what you use to calculate 17 times 24 or fill in a tax form. Most of the time, System 1 serves us well. The problem is that it's not so much accurate as confident. It jumps to conclusions, relies on rules of thumb and is easily influenced by irrelevant information — a number you saw a minute ago, for example, can affect your estimate of something completely unrelated. That's called anchoring. System 2 can correct these errors, but it's lazy; it takes effort, and we're often happy to accept the first answer that comes to mind. The lesson isn't that intuition is useless. It's that, the higher the stakes, the more it pays to slow down.

It is natural to assume that expertise protects us from error. The more we know about a subject, surely, the better our judgements become. In many domains, this is true: an experienced radiologist is far more likely to spot a tumour than a beginner, and a chess grandmaster sees patterns invisible to a novice. Yet research on expert judgement offers a more complicated picture. In a famous long-term study, the political scientist Philip Tetlock collected thousands of predictions from experts in politics and economics over many years. When he compared their forecasts with what actually happened, the results were sobering. Many experts performed only slightly better than chance, and in some cases no better than simple statistical rules. Strikingly, the most famous experts — those most often quoted in the media — were often among the least accurate. Tetlock drew on an image from the philosopher Isaiah Berlin to explain the difference. "Hedgehogs" know one big thing: they view the world through a single theory and make bold, confident predictions. "Foxes" know many small things: they draw on multiple perspectives, are comfortable with uncertainty and readily change their minds. On average, foxes made more accurate forecasts. Hedgehogs, however, were all the more appealing to audiences precisely because of their confidence. The lesson is not so much that experts are useless as that confidence and accuracy are by no means the same thing. Indeed, the Dunning–Kruger effect — the finding that people with limited knowledge in a field tend to overestimate their competence — suggests that confidence can sometimes be a sign of ignorance rather than mastery. The best thinkers, it seems, are every bit as knowledgeable as the boldest ones, but nowhere near as certain. For those of us who listen to experts, the implication is clear: be wary of anyone who is never in doubt.

Free indirect speech is so common in modern fiction that we hardly notice it. But it wasn't always there. Scholars often point to Jane Austen, writing in the early nineteenth century, as one of the first novelists in English to use it with real sophistication. In her novels, the narrator's voice slides almost imperceptibly into a character's thoughts — and back out again — so that we see the world through a character's eyes while also sensing the narrator's ironic distance. A century later, modernist writers like Virginia Woolf and James Joyce pushed the technique further, towards what's called stream of consciousness: the attempt to represent the flow of thought itself, with all its jumps, associations and fragments. In Brazilian literature, writers like Graciliano Ramos and Clarice Lispector explored similar territory. What all these writers share is a fascination with the gap between what people say and what they think — and the conviction that fiction is uniquely able to show us both.

"It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." Few opening lines in English literature are as famous as the first sentence of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, published in 1813. Read quickly, it sounds like a solemn general statement. Read carefully, it is something far more slippery. Is it really a universal truth? Of course not. The sentence is ironic: what it describes is not a law of nature but the belief — or rather the hope — of the families with unmarried daughters who populate the novel. The next sentence confirms the joke: the "truth", we learn, is fixed in the minds of the neighbours, who regard any wealthy newcomer as "the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters". The real subject of the opening, then, is not rich men but the society that schemes to marry them. This ability to say one thing while meaning another — to adopt the voice of a character or a community while quietly mocking it — is at the heart of Austen's art, and it depends heavily on free indirect speech. Throughout the novel, the narrator moves in and out of characters' minds, especially that of the heroine, Elizabeth Bennet. We share her quick judgements and sharp observations, and we only gradually realize, as she does, how mistaken some of them are. The reader experiences prejudice from the inside before recognizing it from the outside. Two centuries later, the technique remains one of the most powerful tools available to novelists. It allows fiction to do something that no other art form can do so easily: to place us simultaneously inside and outside another person's mind. To read like a writer is, in large part, to learn to hear those two voices at once — and to ask, at every turn, whose voice we are really hearing.

Why do children learn nursery rhymes so easily? Why do advertising jingles get stuck in our heads? Sound patterns like rhyme, rhythm and alliteration make language easier to process and to remember — which is why oral traditions all over the world, from ancient epic poetry to Brazilian cordel, relied on them long before writing was common. But there's a more surprising effect. In a study published in 2000, psychologists Matthew McGlone and Jessica Tofighbakhsh presented people with sayings in two versions: one that rhymed, like "Woes unite foes", and one that meant the same thing but didn't rhyme, like "Woes unite enemies". Participants judged the rhyming versions to be more accurate. Researchers sometimes call this the "rhyme-as-reason" effect. The sound of a statement, it seems, can influence whether we believe it. Which is a useful thing to know — both if you're writing a slogan, and if you're trying not to be fooled by one.

For most of human history, poetry was something heard rather than read. Long before printed books, communities preserved their histories, laws and stories in verse, recited from memory by bards, griots and storytellers. Rhythm, rhyme and repetition were not decorations but tools: they made long texts easier to memorize and more pleasurable to hear. The Old English epic Beowulf, for instance, relies on heavy alliteration, each line typically linking two or three stressed words that begin with the same sound. Printing gradually changed the relationship between poetry and sound. As poems came to be read silently on the page, poets began to experiment with visual effects — line breaks, spacing, even the shape of the text. By the twentieth century, many poets had abandoned regular metre and rhyme altogether in favour of free verse, which follows the rhythms of natural speech rather than a fixed pattern. Some critics complained that poetry had lost its music, and with it much of its audience. In recent decades, however, the ear has made a remarkable comeback. Spoken word and slam poetry, performed live and shared online, have attracted a new generation of poets and listeners, many of whom would never have opened a poetry anthology. Hip-hop, with its intricate internal rhymes and rhythmic complexity, has been described by many critics as one of the most significant poetic forms of our time. In Brazil, repentistas improvising in verse, cordel writers and slam competitions in city squares have kept the oral tradition vividly alive. Perhaps the lesson is that poetry has never really stopped being music. Even the quietest poem on a page asks to be heard, if only in the reader's head. To read poetry well — in any language — is to listen as much as to look.

Few punctuation marks inspire as much passion as the semicolon. Kurt Vonnegut famously advised writers not to use them at all, mocking them as pretentious — before, with typical irony, using one himself a few pages later. Other writers adore them. To their fans, the semicolon is the most elegant mark in the language: stronger than a comma, gentler than a full stop, it joins two ideas that belong together without forcing them into a single sentence. The truth, as usual, lies somewhere in between. Overused, semicolons can make writing feel heavy and academic. Used well, they create subtle connections that no other mark can manage. My advice? Before you use one, ask yourself a simple question: could each side stand alone as a sentence? If not, it's the wrong mark. And if yes — ask whether the two ideas are close enough to share a breath. If they are, go ahead. If not, a full stop will do the job; it usually does.

Writers have long understood that prose, like music, has rhythm, and that rhythm depends not only on words but on the shape of sentences. In a much-quoted passage from his book The Way We Write, the American writing teacher Gary Provost demonstrated this with a simple experiment. He wrote a paragraph composed entirely of five-word sentences. It was grammatically perfect. It was also, as he pointed out, monotonous. Then he varied the length: a short sentence, a medium one, and then a long, rolling sentence that built and built until it reached its climax. The second version, he argued, did not merely inform; it sang. The lesson is easily overlooked by learners, who often focus on accuracy at the expense of rhythm. A text made entirely of short sentences can sound childish or breathless. A text made entirely of long, complex sentences can exhaust the reader, however impressive each individual sentence may be. The most effective writers alternate. They use long, cumulative sentences to describe and accumulate detail, allowing the reader to settle into a scene; they use periodic sentences, which delay the main point until the end, to build suspense; and they use short sentences — sometimes no more than a word or two — for emphasis, surprise or finality. Punctuation is the instrument that makes this possible. The comma lets a sentence breathe. The semicolon holds two ideas in balance. The colon creates expectation: something important is coming. The dash interrupts, adds, surprises. And the full stop, the most underestimated of all, gives the reader a moment of silence in which a sentence can resonate. None of this can be learned from rules alone. It must be heard. Reading good prose aloud, slowly, remains one of the best ways to develop an ear for rhythm. So does reading your own writing aloud. If you run out of breath, the sentence is too long. If it sounds like a list, it probably needs a variation. Try it.

People sometimes assume that a critic's job is simply to tell you whether something is good or bad. That's the least interesting part of it. A good critic does three things. First, they describe the work vividly enough that you can imagine it, without giving away what shouldn't be given away. Second, they analyse — they explain how the work achieves its effects, or why it fails to. And third, they place it in context: what is this artist trying to do, how does it relate to their earlier work, or to the tradition it belongs to? The verdict comes last, and it should feel earned. The worst reviews, in my experience, are the ones that are either entirely gushing or entirely dismissive. Real works of art are rarely perfect or worthless. Even a masterpiece has weaknesses; even a failure may contain moments of genuine brilliance. A critic's real value lies in noticing both — and in helping readers see what they might otherwise have missed.

Few debut novels arrive with as much expectation as The House of the Two Rivers, the first book by the Manaus-born writer Helena Barros. Shortlisted for a major prize before its publication in English, it has been described by its publishers as "the great Amazonian family saga". It is not quite that — but it is something more interesting.. . The novel follows three generations of the Andrade family, rubber merchants whose fortunes rise and fall with the boom and collapse of the trade in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. At its centre is the family's crumbling mansion, built where two rivers meet, and Dona Clara, the formidable matriarch who refuses to leave it even as the city around her decays.. . Barros is at her best when she slows down. Her descriptions of the river at dawn, of the humid stillness of the house in the afternoon, of the small rituals of a family pretending nothing has changed, are luminous. Her prose is understated yet precise, and her use of free indirect speech allows us to inhabit Clara's mind while quietly exposing her illusions. The scenes between Clara and her granddaughter, in particular, are a masterclass in what goes unsaid.. . The novel is less assured when it tries to cover too much ground. A subplot involving a foreign engineer feels heavy-handed, and the final section, which jumps abruptly to the 1970s, reads more like an epilogue than a conclusion. At over five hundred pages, the book occasionally sags, and a firmer editorial hand might have produced a tighter, more powerful novel.. . For all its flaws, however, this is an accomplished and haunting debut. What it lacks in structural discipline, it more than makes up for in atmosphere, emotional intelligence and sheer beauty of language. Readers who enjoy slow, immersive fiction will find much to admire. Barros is a writer to watch; her second novel may well be a masterpiece.

People often ask me who decides whether a word is "real". The honest answer is: nobody — and everybody. Dictionaries of English don't create words, and they don't approve them. They observe them. Lexicographers track huge collections of real language — books, newspapers, websites, transcripts — looking for words that are being used widely, by many different people, over a sustained period. A word that appears once in a viral post and then disappears won't make it. But if a word keeps appearing in different contexts, across different types of writing, for several years, it's likely to be added. That's how words like "selfie", "emoji" and "podcast" found their way into major dictionaries. This is quite different from languages that have official academies — Portuguese and French, for example, have institutions that publish official vocabularies or spelling rules. English has never had an equivalent. Its dictionaries are descriptive: they tell you how people actually use the language, not how they ought to.

Complaints about the decline of the English language are almost as old as the language itself. In the eighteenth century, Jonathan Swift lamented the "corruptions" introduced by fashionable young writers and proposed an academy to fix the language once and for all. Two centuries later, critics worried about the influence of American films; more recently, the targets have been text messages, social media and teenagers. Each generation, it seems, is convinced that it is witnessing the end of proper English. Linguists tend to be considerably more relaxed. From their perspective, change is not a sign of decay but a condition of life. Every living language constantly gains new words and loses old ones, shifts its pronunciation and adjusts its grammar. Many words now considered perfectly respectable began as slang or as "errors". "Mob", for example, was once a disreputable abbreviation of the Latin mobile vulgus; "nice" originally meant "foolish"; and the verb "to contact", now indispensable in any office, was widely condemned as vulgar American usage in the early twentieth century. The digital age has undoubtedly accelerated the process. New words can now spread across the globe in days rather than decades, and the boundaries between speech and writing have blurred. Yet research on young people's writing has generally found little evidence that texting damages literacy; some studies even suggest that playful abbreviation requires a sophisticated awareness of how language works. None of this means that every innovation deserves to survive, or that standards no longer matter. Clear, precise language remains essential in law, science and public life, and most speakers are perfectly capable of switching between registers. The real skill, perhaps, is not resisting change but navigating it: knowing when "ghosting" is the perfect word, and when it would be entirely out of place.

The linguist Braj Kachru, who was born in Kashmir and worked in the United States, proposed an influential model of English around the world, often pictured as three concentric circles. The inner circle includes countries where English is the main first language: the UK, the US, Australia and so on. The outer circle includes countries where English has an official or institutional role as a second language, often as a result of colonial history: India, Nigeria, Singapore, the Philippines. And the expanding circle includes countries where English is learned as a foreign language for international communication — Brazil, China, Japan, Germany, and most of the world. The model has been criticized and revised, but its central insight remains powerful: English no longer belongs only to its native speakers. In fact, most interactions in English today probably take place between people for whom it isn't a first language at all. Which raises a fascinating question: who, now, sets the standard?

For decades, many language learners have pursued a single, elusive goal: to sound like a native speaker. Textbooks offered recordings in "standard" British or American accents; learners practised minimal pairs late into the night; and those who failed to eliminate every trace of their first language often felt that they had, in some sense, failed. In recent years, this ideal has come under sustained criticism. The first problem is practical. There is no single native accent to imitate. A speaker from Glasgow sounds very different from one from London, Dublin, Texas or Sydney, and none of these accents is inherently more correct than the others. Even the "standard" British accent traditionally taught to learners, Received Pronunciation, is spoken natively by only a small minority of people in the United Kingdom. The second problem concerns purpose. For the vast majority of learners, English is a means of communicating with people from many different countries, most of whom are not native speakers themselves. In these situations, what matters is not whether one sounds British or American but whether one is understood. Research on English as a lingua franca has suggested that certain features — word stress, the distinction between some long and short vowels, and a number of consonant sounds — are far more important for intelligibility than others. A Brazilian speaker who pronounces "think" as "fink" will almost always be understood; one who misplaces the stress in "comfortable" or "development" may cause genuine confusion. None of this means that pronunciation does not matter. Clear pronunciation is a courtesy to one's listeners, and many learners find great satisfaction in mastering the sounds of a new language. But the goal has shifted from imitation to intelligibility, and from shame to confidence. An accent, after all, is not a defect. It is a sign that someone has learned to live in more than one language — which is, by any measure, an achievement.

On 10 December 1948, the General Assembly of the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Drafted in the aftermath of the Second World War, it set out, for the first time, a list of rights that all human beings are entitled to, regardless of nationality, race, sex, religion or any other status. The committee that drafted it was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, and it included representatives from many countries and traditions. Its thirty articles cover civil and political rights — such as the right to life, liberty and a fair trial — as well as economic, social and cultural rights, including the right to education and to work. Notice the language: "No one shall be held in slavery"; "Everyone has the right to education". Technically, the Declaration itself is not a binding treaty. But it has inspired many later legally binding agreements and national constitutions, including Brazil's 1988 Constitution. It has also been translated into more languages than almost any other document in the world.

Drafted in the aftermath of the Second World War, it set out, for the first time, a list of rights that all human beings are entitled to, regardless of nationality, race, sex, religion or any other status. The committee that drafted it was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, and it included representatives from many countries and traditions. Its thirty articles cover civil and political rights — such as the right to life, liberty and a fair trial — as well as economic, social and cultural rights, including the right to education and to work. Notice the language: "No one shall be held in slavery"; "Everyone has the right to education". Technically, the Declaration itself is not a binding treaty. But it has inspired many later legally binding agreements and national constitutions, including Brazil's 1988 Constitution. It has also been translated into more languages than almost any other document in the world.

When the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was drafted in 1948, its authors could not have imagined smartphones, social media or artificial intelligence. Yet many of the most urgent debates about rights today concern precisely these technologies. Article 12 of the Declaration states that no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with their privacy. What does that mean in a world where vast amounts of personal data are collected, analysed and sold, often without users fully understanding what they have agreed to? In response, a growing number of jurisdictions have adopted data protection laws. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which came into force in 2018, has been particularly influential; Brazil's own General Data Protection Law (LGPD) followed shortly afterwards. Under such laws, individuals are typically entitled to know what data is held about them, to request its correction and, in certain circumstances, to have it deleted. Organizations that process data are obliged to have a legal basis for doing so and may be liable to substantial fines if they fail to protect it. New questions continue to emerge. Should people have a right to an explanation when an algorithm denies them a loan or a job? Is internet access itself becoming a basic right, given that so many essential services now depend on it? To what extent should platforms be held liable for harmful content posted by their users? These debates are far from settled. What is clear is that rights are not fixed for all time. They are interpreted, extended and sometimes contested as societies change. The language of the law may sound timeless — "shall", "entitled", "liable" — but the questions it must answer are constantly new.

I've got five minutes before the board meeting. Can you give me the gist of those two reports on the four-day week?
Sure. In a nutshell: the first, from the consultancy, is very positive. It argues that a shorter week boosts productivity and reduces burnout, and it recommends a company-wide trial.
And the second?
The finance team's report takes issue with that. It doesn't dispute the well-being benefits, but it warns that customer service could suffer, especially in our call centres.
So where do they agree?
Both concur that staff are exhausted and that something needs to change. Where they diverge is on the solution — and the risk.
What's your view?

Homework, in my view, remains an essential part of learning. It reinforces what students have studied in class, develops independent study habits and gives parents a window into their children's education. Without it, many pupils would simply forget what they had learned. The problem is not homework itself but bad homework: repetitive tasks that take hours and teach nothing new.

I'd go further. The research on homework, particularly for younger children, is mixed at best. Some studies suggest a modest benefit for older students, but for primary school pupils, the evidence is weak. Meanwhile, homework can increase stress and inequality: children with educated parents and quiet places to study benefit, while others fall further behind. I'd abolish it for under-twelves and drastically reduce it for everyone else.

Text 1 — The case for tourism. For many regions, tourism is not merely an industry but a lifeline. It brings income to places where few other opportunities exist, creates jobs for young people who might otherwise be forced to migrate, and provides funding for the preservation of historic buildings and natural landscapes. Moreover, travel broadens the mind: visitors who encounter other cultures at first hand often return home more tolerant and curious. To condemn tourism wholesale, as some critics now do, is to ignore the livelihoods of millions and the very real benefits of human contact across borders.. . Text 2 — The cost of popularity. Across the world, a growing number of cities and natural sites are struggling under the weight of their own popularity. In some historic centres, short-term rentals have driven up housing costs so steeply that local residents can no longer afford to live there; neighbourhoods once full of life now resemble theme parks. Fragile ecosystems are damaged by crowds, and much of the money generated by tourism flows to international companies rather than local communities. This is not an argument against travel itself, but against an unregulated model that treats places as products. Without limits, tourism risks destroying the very things that make destinations worth visiting.. . Model essay. Both texts address the impact of tourism on the places that receive it, but they reach rather different conclusions.. . The first writer presents tourism as vital for many communities, arguing that it generates income and employment in areas with few alternatives and helps finance the conservation of heritage and nature. The text also emphasizes the cultural value of travel, suggesting that contact with other ways of life fosters open-mindedness. While these points are undoubtedly valid, the writer arguably overstates the case by dismissing critics so readily.. . The second text, by contrast, focuses on the consequences of excessive tourism. Its author contends that soaring demand for holiday accommodation has priced residents out of their own neighbourhoods, that natural environments are suffering, and that the economic benefits often bypass local people. Crucially, however, the writer does not reject travel as such, but rather a model that lacks regulation.. . In my view, the second text offers the more nuanced analysis. It acknowledges, at least implicitly, the advantages highlighted in the first text, while identifying real problems that a purely positive account ignores. The challenge, as I see it, is not to choose between tourism and its critics, but to strike a balance: to welcome visitors while ensuring that communities retain control over their homes, their environment and their economy.

In 1990, a Stanford graduate student named Elizabeth Newton ran a simple experiment. She divided participants into "tappers" and "listeners". The tappers were asked to tap out the rhythm of a well-known song, like "Happy Birthday", on a table, and the listeners had to guess the song. Before starting, the tappers predicted that listeners would guess correctly about half the time. In reality, listeners identified only around 1 in 40 songs. Why the huge gap? Because when the tappers tapped, they heard the melody in their heads. They simply couldn't imagine what it was like to hear only the knocking. This is what's often called the curse of knowledge: once we know something, it's extremely difficult to remember what it's like not to know it. Experts fall into this trap constantly. They skip steps, use jargon and assume background knowledge that their audience doesn't have. The cure isn't to know less. It's to test your explanations on real people — and to watch their faces, not your slides.

For decades, language teaching tended to focus on four skills: reading, writing, listening and speaking. When the Council of Europe published an expanded version of the Common European Framework of Reference in 2020 — the so-called Companion Volume — it gave unprecedented prominence to a further area: mediation. In the framework's terms, mediation involves acting as an intermediary, making communication possible between people who, for linguistic, cultural or other reasons, would otherwise struggle to understand one another. This might mean relaying information from a text in one language to someone who speaks another, explaining complex data to a non-specialist, or facilitating a discussion between colleagues with conflicting views. The shift reflects a broader recognition of how language is actually used in the modern world. Few professionals simply receive and produce messages; most spend a considerable part of their day processing information from one source and adapting it for another audience. A lawyer explains a contract to a client; a nurse translates medical instructions into everyday language; a project manager summarizes a technical report for the board; a bilingual employee bridges the gap between a foreign head office and a local team. In each case, success depends not on knowing the most sophisticated words but on choosing the right words for the right listener. At the highest levels of proficiency, the CEFR descriptors for mediation are notably demanding. A C2 user is expected to be able to explain, in clear and fluent language, the way facts and arguments are presented in a text, to convey subtle nuances of attitude and opinion, and to adapt their language flexibly to different audiences. In other words, mastery of a language is no longer defined only by what one can understand and say, but by what one can help others to understand. It is, perhaps, the most generous definition of fluency yet devised.

Most people fear impromptu questions more than prepared speeches. The good news is that answering well off the cuff is a skill you can practise. Here's a simple structure I teach. First, pause. A two-second silence feels like an eternity to you, but to the audience it signals that you're taking the question seriously. Second, acknowledge the question: "That's an important point." Third, give your answer in one clear sentence — the headline. Fourth, support it with a reason or an example. And fifth, stop. The biggest mistake people make isn't saying too little; it's saying too much, circling around until they've lost their train of thought. If you genuinely don't know, say so: "I don't know, but here's how I'd find out." Paradoxically, admitting uncertainty with composure often makes you seem more confident, not less. Remember, the audience isn't hoping you'll fail. They want you to rise to the occasion.

Ask a group of advanced learners what fluency means and many will describe something close to perfection: speaking without hesitation, without errors, without ever searching for a word. By that standard, very few native speakers would qualify. Recordings of spontaneous conversation reveal that native speakers hesitate constantly. They start sentences and abandon them, repeat words, correct themselves mid-phrase and fill pauses with "um", "you know" and "I mean". Research on spoken grammar, drawing on large collections of real conversation, has shown that much of everyday speech consists of fragments and false starts that would be marked as errors in a written exam. Why, then, do native speakers sound fluent? Part of the answer is that they manage these disruptions smoothly. Their hesitations fall in natural places — before an important word, rather than in the middle of a fixed phrase. Their self-corrections are quick and unselfconscious. They have a large repertoire of chunks and strategies that keep the conversation moving while they think: "the thing is", "how can I put it", "what I'm trying to say is". In other words, fluency is not the absence of difficulty but the ability to handle it. This has important implications for learners. Many advanced students, anxious to avoid mistakes, adopt strategies that actually make them sound less fluent: they speak slowly and carefully, avoid complex structures and fall silent when they cannot find the perfect word. Paradoxically, they would sound more natural if they allowed themselves to hesitate, rephrase and correct themselves as native speakers do. The goal at the highest level, then, is not to eliminate imperfection but to make it invisible — or, better still, irrelevant. A speaker who loses a word and says, without embarrassment, "What's the word I'm looking for... the thing you use to open a bottle?" has not failed. She has demonstrated exactly the kind of flexibility that defines mastery.

Slang has a curious life cycle. It usually begins within a specific group — teenagers, musicians, gamers, a particular neighbourhood — as a way of signalling belonging. Using the right words shows you're an insider. But slang is a victim of its own success. As it spreads, through music, films and especially social media, outsiders start using it too: parents, advertisers, politicians trying to sound young. And the moment that happens, it loses its value as a marker of the group, so the group moves on to something new. That's why slang can seem to change almost every year, and why words that sounded cool to one generation sound embarrassing to the next. Interestingly, a few slang words escape this cycle and become standard English. "Mob", "bus", "cool" and "OK" were all once considered informal or slang. Others, like "groovy" or "rad", become firmly attached to a particular decade. For learners, the lesson is simple: understand slang, enjoy it — but be careful about adopting it, because you may be wearing last year's fashion without realizing it.

Modern English has one second-person pronoun: you. Whether we are addressing a child, a stranger, a president or a crowd of thousands, the same word serves. It was not always so. In Middle and Early Modern English, speakers could choose between two forms, much as speakers of Portuguese, French or German still can. "Thou" (with its forms thee, thy and thine) was used in the singular, while "you" (or "ye") was originally plural. Over time, influenced partly by French usage, "you" also came to be used as a polite form for addressing a single social superior, while "thou" was reserved for intimates, children, inferiors — or for deliberate insult. Shakespeare's characters switch between the two with considerable subtlety. A lover may move from the respectful "you" to the tender "thou" at a moment of intimacy; a master may address a servant as "thou" while expecting "you" in return; and to "thou" a stranger could be a calculated provocation. Audiences of the time would have registered these shifts instantly, much as a Brazilian notices the difference between "você" and "o senhor". By the eighteenth century, however, "thou" had largely disappeared from standard English, surviving mainly in regional dialects, in religious language and among groups such as the Quakers, who deliberately used it for everyone as a statement of equality. The irony is that "thou", once the form of intimacy and familiarity, now sounds to most English speakers solemn, distant and archaic — the language of prayers and old poetry. The loss of the distinction has had an interesting consequence. Since English can no longer signal social distance through its pronouns, it does so through other means: titles, first names versus surnames, modal verbs, indirectness and the choice of vocabulary. Politeness in English, in other words, did not disappear with "thou". It simply moved elsewhere — into the subtleties of register that every advanced learner must eventually master.

Luana, here is your card. The question is: "What role should tradition play in modern society?" You have two minutes.

That's a question I've given a fair amount of thought to, partly because Brazil is a country where tradition and modernity coexist in fascinating ways. I'd argue that tradition is not so much a set of rules to be obeyed as a resource to be drawn on. Take festivals such as the festas juninas: they connect urban families to their rural roots, and yet they're constantly being reinvented. That, to my mind, is tradition at its best — alive, adaptable and shared. Having said that, tradition can also be used to justify exclusion. Practices that were once considered "natural" — about gender roles, for instance — have rightly been questioned. So the real challenge, I think, is to distinguish between traditions that bind communities together and those that merely preserve inequality. In short, I'd say tradition deserves respect, but never blind obedience.
Thank you. Rafael, do you agree?

Largely, yes — though if anything, I'd push the point further. Far be it from me to sound pessimistic, but I think globalization is eroding many local traditions faster than communities can reinvent them.
That's a fair point, but couldn't one argue that globalization also gives traditions a new audience? Brazilian capoeira, for example, is now practised all over the world.
True — though one might ask whether it remains the same tradition once it's been exported and, to some extent, commercialized.

People often ask me what happens after C2. Is there a level beyond mastery? Officially, no — the CEFR stops here. But anyone who has reached this level knows that learning doesn't stop. In fact, in some ways it becomes more interesting. At C2, you're no longer learning the language; you're learning through it. You read novels for pleasure, not practice. You notice how a politician's choice of words reveals more than they intended. You make a joke that lands perfectly, and nobody thinks to praise your English, because your English has become invisible. That, I think, is the real mark of mastery: when the language stops being an obstacle between you and the world and becomes a window onto it. And yet there will always be a word you've never heard, an accent that puzzles you, an idiom that makes you smile. Native speakers experience this too. Language is too vast to ever be fully conquered. Perhaps that's the most beautiful thing about it.

The Common European Framework of Reference describes the C2 user in a handful of carefully chosen phrases: someone who can understand with ease virtually everything heard or read, summarize information from different sources, reconstructing arguments and accounts in a coherent presentation, and express themselves spontaneously, very fluently and precisely, differentiating finer shades of meaning even in the most complex situations. Each phrase rewards closer attention. "With ease" suggests that comprehension is no longer an effort but a habit. "Reconstructing arguments" implies not merely understanding a text but being able to rebuild its logic in one's own words for someone else. "Spontaneously" means without preparation — in the meeting, at the dinner table, in the unexpected moment. And "finer shades of meaning" points to the domain in which C2 differs most from every level below: nuance. A B2 learner knows that "stubborn" and "determined" are related. A C1 learner knows that one is negative and one is positive. A C2 user knows when to choose "determined" in a reference letter in order to describe, diplomatically, someone who was in fact rather stubborn — and understands the same move when others make it. It is worth noting what the descriptors do not say. They do not require the C2 user to sound like a native speaker, to have no accent, or never to make a mistake. Many C2 users retain a clear accent; many native speakers would struggle with C2 reading tasks. Mastery, in the framework's terms, is defined not by origin but by capability — by what one can do with the language.
